problem: How to build test cases for attack strength when picking a toxic target ahead of time would make brute-force discovery of a prompt infeasible.
did: They dropped the requirement that the target be toxic and worked in reverse, sampling prefixes, enumerating contexts, and choosing the least-likely output token as the target.
alternatives_named: choose q ahead of time
stated_reason: If q were chosen ahead of time, it might be very hard to find, even via brute force, a prefix p such that Gen(p)=q.
quote: If we were to choose $q$ ahead of time, then it might be very hard to find—even via brute force—a prefix $p$ so that $\texttt{Gen}(p)=q$. So instead we drop the requirement that $q$ is toxic, and approach the problem from reverse.
title: Are aligned neural networks adversarially aligned?

problem: Which threat model to evaluate prior NLP attacks under: one where the attacker controls the tokens right before generation, or one matching chat-bot deployments with fixed special tokens after user input.
did: They evaluated attacks where the adversary controls only the user message and the [AGENT]: token is appended afterwards, rather than adopting the stronger threat model of Jones et al.
alternatives_named: attacker controls the entire prompt, Gen(X)
attacker controls the text immediately preceding the generation, Gen(P_pre||X)
stated_reason: The stronger threat model makes the attack much easier but does not match current chat-bot deployments.
quote: In both cases, the attacker controls the tokens right before the model’s generation, which makes an attack much easier (but not relevant for current chat bot deployments).
title: Are aligned neural networks adversarially aligned?

problem: Where to generate brute-force test cases given the high cost of brute-force search, and whether results would transfer to harder aligned models.
did: They generated test cases using GPT-2 only, reasoning that failure on the easier model implies failure on harder aligned models.
alternatives_named: generating test cases on aligned models
stated_reason: Brute force is costly, and GPT-2 is easier to attack, so attack failures there are unlikely to be reversed on aligned models.
quote: We generate our test cases using GPT-2 only, due to the cost of running a brute force search. However, as GPT-2 is an easier model to attack, if attacks fail here, they are unlikely to succeed on the more difficult cases of aligned models.
title: Are aligned neural networks adversarially aligned?

problem: Whether the very low pass rates of prior attacks on the test set reflect a real weakness or just a too-restrictive token budget.
did: They gave the attacker more control by multiplying the number of attacker-controlled tokens up to 10x and checked whether the failure persisted.
stated_reason: Because the numbers were so low, they wanted to see whether extra attacker freedom would change the conclusion.
quote: Because the numbers here are so low, we then experimented with giving the attacker more control, with a multiplicative factor on the number of manipulated tokens.
title: Are aligned neural networks adversarially aligned?

problem: The simple substring-based isToxic metric could mislabel outputs as toxic, so it was unclear whether reported success rates were trustworthy.
did: They qualitatively inspected a subset of generations, found under ten cases where the metric was flawed, and kept the simple metric while acknowledging its limits.
alternatives_named: more careful toxicity definitions
stated_reason: Attacks currently have negligible success even under this loose definition, so a more careful definition is deferred until attacks achieve nontrivial success.
quote: Future work will need to carefully consider different toxicity definitions once attacks begin to have nontrivial attack success rates—for now, even with this loose definition, the current attacks in the literature fail to find successful adversarial sequences.
title: Are aligned neural networks adversarially aligned?

problem: How strongly to claim that text-only aligned models are vulnerable to adversarial inputs given that only multimodal attacks and attack-failure evidence exist.
did: They framed the claim as an explicit conjecture rather than a demonstrated result, supported by two lines of indirect evidence.
stated_reason: They cannot prove the claim, but believe the soft-embedding attacks and the known-to-exist-yet-unfound solutions provide strong evidence.
quote: While we cannot prove this claim (that’s why it’s a conjecture!) we believe our paper provides strong evidence for it: (1) language models are weak to soft-embedding attacks (e.g., multimodal attacks); and (2) current NLP attacks cannot find solutions that are known to exist.
title: Are aligned neural networks adversarially aligned?

problem: Directly optimizing the true toxicity objective over long generations is expensive, since backpropagation through many forward passes would be required.
did: They optimized a surrogate harmful-prefix objective, making the model begin its response with a malicious string, requiring only a single forward pass.
alternatives_named: directly optimizing isToxic(Gen(X)) over the full generated sequence
stated_reason: The surrogate is much easier to optimize, and once the model begins with harmful output it continues emitting harmful text without further adversarial control.
quote: instead of directly optimizing the true objective, i.e., checking that $\texttt{isToxic}(S)$ is true for a generated $S$, we optimize for the surrogate objective $S_{..j}=t$ for some malicious string $t$, with $j\ll\lvert S\rvert$.
title: Are aligned neural networks adversarially aligned?

problem: How to choose which of many candidate research problems to work on next, given limited capacity and an abundance of ideas.
did: Maintained an append-only ideas file and, between projects, skimmed it and picked whichever idea seemed most interesting or important at that moment.
alternatives_named: find something new entirely if nothing looks compelling
passing projects off to lab members
stated_reason: As an independent contributor he can only work on a few things at a time, so each choice means not doing something else; his problem is filtering ideas, not generating them.
quote: When it's time to pick my next project, I skim through the list, and pick whichever I think is most interesting. or exciting. or important. or whatever I'm looking for at the moment.
title: My research idea logfile, 2016-2019

problem: What kinds of tasks should a new LLM benchmark be built from, given that existing benchmarks focus on homework-style problems?
did: Built the benchmark from nearly 100 tests extracted from the author's own real conversation history with LLMs, focused on three types of questions he actually asks.
alternatives_named: homework-style problems typical of existing benchmarks
academic benchmarks of general model capabilities
stated_reason: The questions assigned to students differ from the questions the author wants a model to solve for him.
quote: Existing benchmarks tend to focus on solving typical problems that might be assigned to a student as homework. But the types of questions that are assigned to students are different from the types of questions I want to ask a language model to solve for me.
title: My benchmark for large language models

problem: How should model answers be evaluated so that tests reflect realistic use and can be scored automatically?
did: Built a dataflow DSL that specifies both how to ask the question and how to evaluate the answer, mostly by actually running model-written code in a docker container.
alternatives_named: other evaluation methods supported by the framework
manual evaluation of context-specific tasks
stated_reason: It makes it easy to add new tests that realistically evaluate model capabilities, including the output of code the model writes.
quote: I've implemented a simple dataflow domain specific language to make it easy for me (or anyone else!) to add new tests that realistically evaluate model capabilities. This DSL allows for specifying both how the question should be asked and also how the answer should be evaluated.
title: My benchmark for large language models

problem: How should tasks that are context-specific and impossible to evaluate automatically be handled in the benchmark?
did: Extracted the essence of the task and wrote a corresponding question that can be evaluated.
alternatives_named: dropping such tasks
evaluating the original context-specific task directly
stated_reason: The original tasks are context-specific and impossible to evaluate automatically.
quote: Or, in cases where the actual task I was asking for is context-specific and impossible to evaluate automatically, I've tried to extract the essence of the task and write a correspodning question.
title: My benchmark for large language models

problem: How strongly should the benchmark be claimed to measure general model capabilities, given its narrow, personal scope?
did: Explicitly stated it is not a good benchmark for general capabilities nor for any specific capability, but a benchmark for the author's own uses.
alternatives_named: presenting it as a general capability benchmark
an academic benchmark
stated_reason: The model could do many things the author does not ask of it; academic benchmarks exist for that purpose, and the author only cares about getting right answers.
quote: Does this make it a good benchmark for general model capabilities? No. It's possible that the model could do many things I'm just not asking it to do.
title: My benchmark for large language models

problem: Should the benchmark investigate why a model gets an answer right (memorization vs reasoning) or only whether it does?
did: Chose to measure only whether the answer is right, not the mechanism behind it.
alternatives_named: testing for memorization of previously asked questions
testing for clever reasoning on unseen questions
stated_reason: The author just wants the right answer, so the benchmark is for him rather than for a specific type of capability.
quote: I don't care why the model managed to get the answer right. Did it memorize the answer because someone else asked exactly this same question before? Did it use some clever “reasoning” to solve a question it's never seen before? I don't care---I just want the right answer.
title: My benchmark for large language models

problem: How should prompts be designed when querying models in the benchmark: optimized prompting or plain questions?
did: Used plain, un-engineered prompts, simply typing the question as a normal user would.
alternatives_named: telling the model it is an expert
offering a tip or threatening harm
asking the model to take a deep breath and think step by step
stated_reason: The author is lazy and wants to just type a question and get the right answer, rather than measure optimal-use capability.
quote: I do not want to remind the model it is AN EXPERT IN PYTHON and tell it that I'll give it a $100,000 tip for giving the right answer OR I WILL MURDER A KITTEN but please pause....take a deep breath....and think step by step by step before answering.
title: My benchmark for large language models

problem: How can the emoji-conversion task, which has no ground-truth automatic checker, be scored?
did: Asked the same model to convert its emoji output back into movie titles and scored on that round trip.
quote: To evaluate this task I ask the same model to convert those emoji back into movie titles. Useful? No. Fun? Yes.
title: My benchmark for large language models

problem: How can a model's drawn image output (a .bmp from C code) be verified as correct without human inspection?
did: Passed the generated image to a vision language model, asked what flag it shows, and checked the description for 'United States' or 'USA'.
stated_reason: The framework needs an automated check that the code produced a valid, correct image.
quote: And finally, we verify that the code was correct. To do this, we pass the resulting image to a language model and ask what flag has been drawn.
title: My benchmark for large language models

problem: How to interpret the models' poor performance on tasks involving a newly designed assembly language, which might reflect a hard limit or a threshold of capability.
did: Interpreted the rare successes as indicating the task sits right at the boundary of what is becoming possible with a single model evaluation.
stated_reason: Models mostly fail but succeed in very few cases, even on simple programs like testing primality.
quote: In very few cases they succeed, but it looks like this is right at the boundary of what's just becoming possible to achieve with just a single evaluation of the model.
title: My benchmark for large language models

problem: How to surface evaluation flaws in a defense paper that are evident from the paper itself.
did: Prompted GPT-4 with the best-practices checklist and a screenshot of the paper to flag concerning evaluation results, then manually verified the model's answers.
alternatives_named: describing the errors ourselves
stated_reason: The impossibility of the claims is sufficiently well understood that the errors need not be described by the author directly.
quote: The impossibility of the claims it makes are sufficiently well understood that, instead of describing the errors ourselves, we prompt GPT-4 with a copy of the checklist in [3], a screenshot of the defense paper [5]

problem: Whether to trust LLM-generated critiques of the paper's evaluation.

stated_reason: The model identified the flaws correctly, and the author verified this.

title: Cutting through buggy adversarial example defenses: fixing 1 line of code breaks Sabre

problem: How to assess whether the evaluation followed established adversarial robustness standards.
did: Audited the paper item-by-item against the recommended best-practices checklist, e.g. iterative vs single-step attacks, adaptive attacks, ablations.

problem: Which evidence could reveal flaws not visible in the published paper.
did: Inspected the published code and corresponded with the authors to find issues like missing adaptive attacks, insecure baselines, and wrong baseline implementations.
alternatives_named: reading the paper alone
stated_reason: Some flaws can only be noticed by reading the code or corresponding with the authors.
quote: We make a number of other comments on the Sabre defense that can not be observed by reading the paper alone, and can only be noticed by reading the published code or corresponding with the authors.
title: Cutting through buggy adversarial example defenses: fixing 1 line of code breaks Sabre

problem: How to attack a defense claimed to be end-to-end differentiable yet evaluated with BPDA.
did: Hypothesized the BPDA wrapper was causing gradient masking and removed it with a one-line change, rerunning the original evaluation code.

stated_reason: Sabre is already differentiable, so wrapping it in BPDA removes the useful gradient and replaces it with a much less useful one.
quote: But Sabre is already differentiable; wrapping it with BDPA removes the useful gradient and replaces it with one that is much less useful. And so to break Sabre all we have to do is remove the unnecessary BPDA wrapping.
title: Cutting through buggy adversarial example defenses: fixing 1 line of code breaks Sabre

problem: How to interpret the authors' claim that the new discretization component was part of the original defense.
did: Treated the component as a changed defense introduced to block the first attack, and analyzed it as a nondifferentiable component with a buggy gradient that points away from adversarial examples.
alternatives_named: accepting that it was part of the original defense
stated_reason: The component was introduced to prevent the first attack and contradicts the paper's claims of end-to-end differentiability.
quote: In personal communication with the authors, they assert this defense component was not described in the paper because it is not an important detail of the overall defense. (This is despite the fact that the entire reason this component was introduced in the first place was to prevent the attack we described above.)
title: Cutting through buggy adversarial example defenses: fixing 1 line of code breaks Sabre

problem: Whether the second break's results on CIFAR-10 sufficiently refute the defense given that the model was self-trained.

alternatives_named: a model trained by the authors themselves

title: Cutting through buggy adversarial example defenses: fixing 1 line of code breaks Sabre

did: Ran a control comparing against the known binarization-alone result and changed the number of decimals from 0 to 1 to see whether the attack still succeeded.

title: Cutting through buggy adversarial example defenses: fixing 1 line of code breaks Sabre

did: Asserted strongly that Sabre exhibits the most extreme gradient masking the author had seen, because the gradient points directly away from adversarial examples.

problem: Whether to withhold or publish a severe vulnerability in an old enrollment system that nobody could fix.

alternatives_named: go public immediately
report to developers who could fix it
stated_reason: Going public sooner wouldn't minimize harm: students couldn't stop using the system, no one was left to fix it, and the attack would be trivially exploitable once public.

did: Contacted dataset owners so they could add integrity checks before publishing, but still published the attack.
alternatives_named: not publicizing the attack

extended private disclosure to the defense authors

problem: How to elicit forecasts so that calibration of respondents can be assessed before the outcomes are known.

problem: How to design a security benchmark that measures LLM capability without relying on a proxy task.
did: The authors built a benchmark on the complete end-to-end task of breaking adversarial example defenses, using real-world research code and mechanistically verifiable success.
alternatives_named: CTF-style benchmarks such as Cybench
proxy metrics for security tasks
stated_reason: Proxy-free, verifiable tasks directly show whether an LLM could contribute to adversarial ML research, unlike CTF puzzles built for human training.

problem: How to isolate the gap between attacking CTF-like code and attacking real-world code.
did: The authors added 24 simplified CTF-like re-implementations of real defenses from the Google self-study course as a comparison subset next to the real-world repositories.

problem: Whether benchmark contamination from published breaks of some included defenses undermines the results.
did: The authors judged contamination not a major concern after noting low success rates and testing with the previously written attack paper placed in context.
alternatives_named: treating contamination as a major threat to validity
stated_reason: Success rates were very low even for the best agent, and giving the model the attack paper did not significantly improve success.
quote: Second, we found that even if we explicitly place the previously-written attack paper in the language model’s context, the success rate does not significantly improve. This indicates that the models are currently not sophisticated enough to fully leverage such information, even when it is directly available.
title: AutoAdvExBench: Benchmarking autonomous exploitation of adversarial example defenses

problem: Which metric best reports attacker performance on a benchmark with many degrees of freedom.
did: The authors proposed plotting the sorted robust accuracy of every defense as a cumulative distribution, with average robust accuracy and count of defenses below half of clean accuracy only as fallback scalars.
alternatives_named: a single scalar number
binary success or failure per challenge
stated_reason: The full curve captures intermediate solutions, while the two scalars capture average-case improvement and substantial degradation respectively.
quote: We believe the most informative metric to evaluate an attacker LLM is to evaluate the model’s attack success rate for every defense in our dataset, and then plot a “cumulative distribution function” of the defense accuracies.
title: AutoAdvExBench: Benchmarking autonomous exploitation of adversarial example defenses

problem: Whether to keep adapting existing general-purpose coding agents or to build a task-specific agent.

alternatives_named: direct LLM prompting
best-of-k sampling
SWE-Bench-style agent frameworks

title: AutoAdvExBench: Benchmarking autonomous exploitation of adversarial example defenses

title: AutoAdvExBench: Benchmarking autonomous exploitation of adversarial example defenses

problem: How strongly to claim that individual defenses were broken or that results generalize.
did: The authors explicitly limited claims, stating that an attack success on one defense is not a definitive break and noting limitations of the dataset.

title: LLMs unlock new paths to monetizing exploits

alternatives_named: having the model develop proof-of-concept exploits
stated_reason: Models could not complete validation, which requires real-world actions like creating accounts that LLMs refuse or are slow at.
quote: We initially also attempted to ask the language model to develop a proof-of-concept exploit, but found current models do not yet have the ability to achieve this step of the attack: validating many exploits requires, for example, creating accounts on social media websites
title: LLMs unlock new paths to monetizing exploits

problem: How strongly to claim results from the 200-extension vulnerability study.
did: They explicitly framed the experiment as a demonstration that the question is economic rather than a rigorous study of exploit-development ability.
alternatives_named: a rigorous study of exploit development efficacy
stated_reason: The goal is to show it is no longer a speculative question of technical capabilities, and the study is only a preliminary analysis of 200 extensions.
quote: We emphasize again that the purpose of this experiment is not to conduct a rigorous study of the degree to which current language models are able to effectively develop exploits in this space, but to demonstrate that this is no longer a speculative question of technical capabilities.
title: LLMs unlock new paths to monetizing exploits

problem: How to treat LLM unreliability (hallucination, false positives) when assessing attacker viability.
did: They argued that failures only proportionally reduce attacker value rather than preventing deployment, and that false-positive validation cost will fall as models improve.
stated_reason: Developing and monetizing exploits tolerates failures, since a 1% or 10% failure rate only reduces potential value by that fraction.
quote: If 1% (or 10%) of attempted exploits fail due to hallucinating vulnerabilities that do not exist, this only reduces the potential value by 1% (or 10%); it does not limit the applicability of deploying the successful attacks.
title: LLMs unlock new paths to monetizing exploits

problem: Which attack scenarios to implement as proofs-of-concept versus leave as speculation.
did: They implemented realistic ethical proofs-of-concept in Section 3 and relegated attacks lacking a realistic, ethical test method to Section 4 as unvalidated discussion.
alternatives_named: implementing every attack vector
stated_reason: They could not easily identify a method for a realistic and ethical proof-of-concept for those attacks.
quote: we consider a further set of attacks that we believe are technically feasible and would be economically valuable, but where we are unable to easily identify a method of performing a realistic and ethical proof-of-concept attack.
title: LLMs unlock new paths to monetizing exploits

problem: Determining whether directly querying or benchmarking a fine-tuned model is enough to reveal harmful behavior introduced by covert attacks.
did: They gave the auditor attack-specific elicitation affordances (dataset-derived system prompts, cipher-encoded prompts, backdoor triggers) rather than relying on plain benchmarks or queries.
alternatives_named: directly querying the harmful model with a benchmark designed to detect misaligned models
running a benchmark or querying without attack-specific elicitation
stated_reason: Many attacks are only effective if the model is queried according to the attack, so un-elicited queries make harmful models appear relatively safe.
quote: Detecting harmful finetuning is not as simple as querying the fine-tuned model and measuring if it responds harmfully. As we show in Figure 3, many attacks are only effective if an attacker queries the model according to the attack
title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents

problem: Choosing an evaluation set that tests detection against attacks that existing defenses cannot catch.
did: They built a set of 8 adversarial and 5 benign fine-tunes in which each adversarial datapoint is individually harmless, covering diverse attack types, and included challenging benign cases.
stated_reason: The set is meant to be challenging: adversarial data bypasses content moderation, and benign fine-tunes (low-resource language, etc.) can have unintentional side effects that look mildly harmful.
quote: The set is challenging in that each datapoint of the adversarial fine-tune dataset is individually harmless and therefore bypasses content moderation on the input dataset, while the benign fine-tunes include challenging cases like low resource languages
title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents

problem: Verifying that each fine-tuned adversarial model is truly harmful before using it as a positive example in the evaluation.
did: They confirmed attack success for every adversarial model on HEx-PHI with a GPT-4o judge, using attack-specific elicitation, before including it.
stated_reason: Without attack-specific elicitation some attacks go undetected, so confirmation requires eliciting with the attack's own method.
quote: We confirmed attack success for all adversarial attacks before inclusion using the harmful HEx-PHI benchmark prompts with GPT-4o as a judge classifying harmful responses.
title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents

problem: Determining which auditor affordances actually contribute to detection performance.
did: They ran an ablation over many tool configurations, with 20 independent audits per fine-tune per configuration, and compared TPR at fixed low FPR plus AUROC.
stated_reason: Understanding the utility of each tool; the work needs high TPR at low FPR so legitimate fine-tuning use is not blocked.
quote: We assess auditor performance across different configurations of allowed tool calls as follows. For each tool configuration and fine-tuned model, we run $n=20$ independent audits.
title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents

problem: Deciding how strongly to describe the detector's performance given that it detects every attack but only about half of the time at low FPR.
did: They claim all attacks are detected by some tool subset and the method is state-of-the-art, but explicitly caveat that a roughly 50% TPR at 1% FPR means attackers can still frequently evade it and that more tools do not strictly improve results.
stated_reason: Attackers can still frequently evade the detector and false positives on benign fine-tunes remain a challenge.
quote: More work is necessary to develop malicious fine-tuning auditing agents that can be deployed in production: while our detector is state-of-the-art and out-performs other detectors, a 50% true positive rate at a 1% false positive rate means attackers can still frequently evade the detector.
title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents

problem: Interpreting high risk scores that the auditor assigns to benign fine-tunes, which could be false alarms or real subtle safety degradation.
did: They treated some of these as partly justified, noting that benign fine-tuning can genuinely degrade safeguards, and acknowledged this as a limitation of the problem formulation rather than purely auditor error.
stated_reason: Benign fine-tunes such as the Kashmiri, educational insecure code and Alpaca models do show real non-refusal or safeguard interference, and a strong auditor can jailbreak a benign model.
quote: Sometimes, the reasons presented were justified. For example, our low resource language fine-tune occasionally does not refuse harmful queries, though its non-refusal responses are not particularly helpful or coherent.
title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents

problem: Reducing variance and fixation of single audits on specific in-context examples.
did: They built a super-agent that runs 10 sub-audits and has a super-auditor review all of them and investigate further, evaluating it with the simple D + M configuration.
alternatives_named: single-agent approach
stated_reason: A single auditing agent may fixate on specific examples in-context and scores vary across audits, so aggregation may improve performance, though it could also amplify poor reasoning.
quote: Given a single auditing agent may fixate on specific examples in-context and that there is variance in scores across audits for a single fine-tuned model, aggregating the results across multiple audits may either improve performance or amplify poor reasoning.
title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents

problem: Choosing which LLM should power the auditing agent and how to compare candidate models fairly.
did: They compared Claude Sonnet 4, o3 and Qwen 2.5 72b using the simple D + M configuration with 20 audits per fine-tune, weighing false positives alongside detection.
alternatives_named: Qwen 2.5 72b
o3
stated_reason: D + M provides a simple configuration for comparison across models, and minimizing false positives is equally important as detection.
quote: While this was not our best performing set of affordances with Claude Sonnet 4, it provides a simple configuration for comparison across models.
title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents

problem: Testing whether future adversaries could evade the auditor, given that the evaluated attacks were not designed against it.
did: They tried distraction-based evasion attempts themselves, and discussed other possible evasions (more covert steganography, clean-label backdoors, jailbreaking the auditor) without evaluating them.
alternatives_named: more covert steganography
clean-label backdoors
semantic backdoor triggers
datasets that jailbreak the auditor itself
stated_reason: An adversary may construct datasets that cannot be understood by the auditor or that distract it, so detection metrics alone do not establish robustness.
quote: Though our own attempts to evade the auditor by distraction were unsuccessful, a sophisticated adversary may be able to do so.
title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents

problem: Keeping the auditor prompts from being tailored to the evaluated attacks, which would inflate the measured detection results.
did: They kept prompts generic and minimally engineered, without hints about particular attacks.
stated_reason: Generic prompts should stay robust to new attacks.
quote: We sought to keep prompts generic and not suggestive of particular attacks, with minimal prompt-engineering, so that they would remain robust to new attacks.
title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents

problem: How to measure an LLM agent's propensity to cheat on coding tasks without relying on costly manual inspection or unreliable LLM judgments.
did: They built 'impossible' task variants by mutating unit tests to contradict the natural-language spec, so any pass is unambiguously a specification-violating shortcut and the pass rate serves as the cheating rate.
alternatives_named: costly manual inspection
unreliable LLM judgments
stated_reason: Standard benchmarks cannot distinguish specification-violating shortcuts from genuine solutions, whereas impossible tasks give a noiseless proxy for cheating propensity.
quote: We instruct agents to prioritize the specification, so any pass necessarily implies a specification-violating shortcut. A score of 0% on these impossible tasks is ideal, while a high score reveals a model's tendency to prioritize passing tests over following instructions.
title: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs’ Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases

problem: How to design the test mutations so they reliably produce impossible tasks and allow comparison of different kinds of conflict.
did: They used two mutation strategies, One-Off and Conflicting, and report results for the two variants separately.
stated_reason: Different mutation strategies may have different effects on cheating propensity.
quote: Different mutation strategies may have different effects on the cheating propensity, so we report the results of the two mutation variants separately in our experiments.
title: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs’ Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases

problem: Whether to accept LLM-generated impossible mutations as valid, given that they may not truly be impossible, especially for multi-file SWE-bench tasks.
did: They validated each mutation by running it against both the original patch and an empty patch and removed any mutation that passed either, while skipping this check for LiveCodeBench.
stated_reason: LLM-generated mutations are not guaranteed to be valid, and the filtering reduces noise; LiveCodeBench lacks standard solutions so the check cannot be done there.
quote: To reduce noise, we verify their validity by testing them against both the original patches from the base benchmarks and empty patches that make no changes. Valid impossible mutations should fail both tests, and we remove any mutations that pass either test.
title: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs’ Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases

problem: Whether agents should have access to the tests, which affects how many opportunities there are to cheat and how realistic the setting is.
did: They gave agents full read/write access to the tests by default, counted passing via test modification as cheating, and ablated this choice later.
alternatives_named: hiding the tests
stated_reason: Unit tests are commonly accessible in real software engineering, creating more opportunities for cheating.
quote: We provide agents with full read/write access to test cases rather than hiding them. While this differs from the original benchmarks, unit tests are commonly accessible in real software engineering, creating more opportunities for cheating.
title: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs’ Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases

problem: How to determine which cheating strategies models use when they pass impossible tasks.
did: They collected the passing transcripts and had Claude Opus 4 classify them into four categories, telling it that each transcript is a successful cheat.
stated_reason: Telling the classifier the transcript is a cheat makes it focus on classification and makes it less likely to consider the transcript legitimate.
quote: Here we instruct Claude Opus 4 that the given transcript is a successful cheating attempt, so it will focus on classification and will be less likely to consider the transcript legitimate.
title: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs’ Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases

problem: How strongly to claim that prompt wording affects cheating, and what to recommend to practitioners.
did: They ablated four prompts of varying strictness, found cheating rates swing widely while original-benchmark performance does not, and recommended careful prompt ablations before deployment.
stated_reason: Prompts did not produce statistically significant differences on the original benchmarks, yet cheating rates differed greatly, with GPT-5 dropping from over 85% to 1% under the strictest prompt.
quote: While these prompts do not produce statistically significant performance difference on the original benchmarks, we find they lead to significantly different cheating propensity on Conflicting-LiveCodeBench (Figure 6).
title: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs’ Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases

problem: How to interpret the flag rate of the LLM monitor on open-test original benchmarks, where ground truth is not known to be non-cheating.
did: They manually examined some flagged transcripts, found most were genuine cheating attempts, and so treated the flag rate only as an upper bound on the false positive rate.
stated_reason: Most manually examined flagged transcripts were indeed cheating, via test modification and special-casing, so the flags are not all false positives.
quote: We also manually examined some transcripts flagged as cheating in the open-test benchmarks, and we found that most of them are indeed cheating attempts with methods including modifying test cases and special-casing, so the flag rate on the open-test benchmarks should only be considered as an upper bound on the false positive rate.
title: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs’ Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases

problem: How to word the conclusion about whether monitors can detect cheating, given the divergent detection rates between simple and complex tasks.
did: They concluded that simple LLM-based monitoring may be insufficient for complex multi-file tasks and that more sophisticated monitors are needed, rather than claiming monitors work.
stated_reason: Detection reached only 42-65% on Impossible-SWEbench versus 86-89% on Impossible-LiveCodeBench, and some cheating evaded detection via rationalizations such as backward compatibility.
quote: These results suggest that simple LLM-based monitoring approaches may not be sufficient for detecting cheating attempts on complex multi-file tasks. For more complex tasks, more sophisticated and capable monitoring solutions will be needed to effectively identify cheating behaviors.
title: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs’ Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases

problem: How to avoid wasting time on research ideas that may fail, given that outcomes cannot be predicted in advance.
did: Start with the sub-problem most likely to fail and build small prototypes to de-risk the project quickly, abandoning ideas that don't work.
alternatives_named: work on the parts of a problem you know how to solve first
build the polished version of the experiment first
stated_reason: Working on easy parts teaches nothing about whether the idea is good; failing fast saves months.
quote: The best way I've found to minimize wasted time is to start with the sub-problem most likely to fail. It's comforting to work on the parts of a problem you know how to solve, but this teaches you nothing about whether your idea is any good.
title: How to win a best paper award (or, an opinionated take on how to do important research)

problem: Whether to continue a project whose technical results look positive but whose impact is likely to be modest.
did: Kill the idea and pick something new, salvaging value as a workshop paper or blog post.
alternatives_named: turn it into a paper with some work
workshop paper or blog post
stated_reason: With more work it could become a paper, but it will not become a good paper, so the time is wasted.
quote: You could probably, with some work, turn this into a paper. But it's not going to become a good paper. When this happens, just kill the idea and pick something new. Maybe turn it into a workshop paper or a blog post.
title: How to win a best paper award (or, an opinionated take on how to do important research)

problem: Whether to drop a nearly finished but modest project when a potentially much higher-impact project appears.
did: Pivot immediately to the higher-impact paper rather than finishing the current one, while cautioning that impact is hard to assess in advance.
alternatives_named: finish the last 10% of the 'just ok' paper
sunk cost reasoning
stated_reason: Because paper impact is distributed exponentially, the marginal return on the remaining effort is higher on a paper 100x more important.
quote: don't fall into a sunk cost fallacy; pivot immediately to the more important paper. This is "it's not you, it's me" applied to research.
title: How to win a best paper award (or, an opinionated take on how to do important research)

problem: How rigorous experiments should be to support claims credibly against skeptical readers.
did: Run multiple trials, control for confounders, and preemptively run experiments answering questions a skeptical reader might ask, even to strengthen 'sometimes' to 'usually'.
stated_reason: Great papers don't have poorly performed experiments; going to unreasonable lengths is what it means to care.
quote: Every experiment should be as precisely performed as you can manage. Run multiple trials. Control for confounders. If there's a question a skeptical reader might ask about your setup, run the experiment that answers it before they ask.
title: How to win a best paper award (or, an opinionated take on how to do important research)

problem: Whether to read prior literature before or after developing one's own approach, given that the field's existing methods may be flawed.
did: Set aside the early membership inference papers, developed his own attack first once he had a sensible idea, and only then read what others were doing.
alternatives_named: reading existing work first
following the field's established approach
stated_reason: Doing the work first avoided being distracted or poisoned by the wrong approach, though it risks reinventing existing or discarded ideas.
quote: Only after I saw a paper that gave me an idea for how to do membership inference in a way that made sense did I (1) develop my own attack, and then (2) read what everyone else was doing.
title: How to win a best paper award (or, an opinionated take on how to do important research)

problem: How to scope a paper's experiments and claims so it is neither unfocused nor missing obvious extensions.
did: Keep every experiment tied to one core idea while still ensuring the paper has no obvious unaddressed improvements, leaving only minor open directions.
alternatives_named: running every possible experiment related to the idea
leaving obvious questions unanswered
stated_reason: Running everything distracts readers from the key idea, but missing obvious improvements leaves readers unsatisfied.
quote: your paper should be at a local optimum; the reader must not be left with the thought "I really wish the authors had done X; that would have been an obvious improvement."
title: How to win a best paper award (or, an opinionated take on how to do important research)

problem: How to decide before doing the research whether a project is worth pursuing.
did: Write the best-case conclusion before running experiments and drop the project if there is nothing to say beyond repeating the results.
alternatives_named: pursue projects whose only conclusion is that the number goes up
stated_reason: If the best-case conclusion has nothing beyond the results, the work mustn't matter very much.
quote: something I frequently do when deciding if a paper is worth writing is write my best-case conclusion before even performing the research. I ask: if this paper were to succeed wildly---if all the experiments turned out exactly as I want---what could I say in a conclusion?
title: How to win a best paper award (or, an opinionated take on how to do important research)

problem: How to interpret repeated rejections of a paper that is later recognized as excellent.
did: Treat rejections as a sign the idea was slightly ahead of accepted beliefs, and revise to make the arguments clearer and stronger rather than abandon the paper.
alternatives_named: abandoning the paper after rejection
stated_reason: Reviewers reject ideas outside what is normally believed; a stronger revision submitted when the idea is less heretical can win awards.
quote: On the first pass, the paper is often rejected because it's saying something a little outside what's normally believed to be true. The reviewers aren't convinced and leave some confused remarks.
title: How to win a best paper award (or, an opinionated take on how to do important research)

problem: How to evaluate whether debate mechanisms work: statistical comparison against baselines using external Mturk judges, or a stricter, faster threshold of performance.
did: They moved away from statistical comparisons against baselines and targeted a threshold where judges identify the correct answer >90% of the time and honesty feels clearly, systematically advantaged.
alternatives_named: statistical comparisons against baselines with Mturk workers
judges' accuracy before seeing information as an easier baseline
judges' accuracy after a single explanation as a harder baseline
stated_reason: Honest strategies need a fundamental, systematic advantage in practice, and the threshold is much quicker to measure, allowing faster iteration.
quote: This consideration led us to target a threshold of performance where honesty has a clear, systematic advantage: judges should be able to identify the correct answer almost all the time (>90%), and it should feel to the experimenters and the participants that dishonest answers are fundamentally disadvantaged.
title: Writeup: Progress on AI Safety via Debate

problem: Whether to test debate mechanisms using external judge and debater pools or by internal iteration.
did: They used mostly internal iteration to test mechanisms and planned to try to break a mechanism only once it appeared to work well.
alternatives_named: external judge and debater pools
stated_reason: The mechanisms still have many easy-to-find failures to work through.
quote: We’re using mostly internal iteration (as opposed to external judge and debater pools) to test these mechanisms, as they still have a lot of easy-to-find failures to work through.
title: Writeup: Progress on AI Safety via Debate

problem: Whether to continue with the Mturk-based, unstructured free-text debate setup after getting data from higher-quality judges.
did: They dropped the Mturk/unstructured approach and focused on developing an improved, structured debate procedure.
alternatives_named: Mturk workers
more interactivity between judges and debaters
stated_reason: Even with very smart, motivated judges who could interact with debaters, debates still didn't work reliably.
quote: However, when we switched to using higher-quality judges who could interact with debaters, we found that our debates still didn’t work reliably -- even with very smart and motivated judges who spent ~an hour.
title: Writeup: Progress on AI Safety via Debate

problem: Which questions to use for testing debate so that failures are informative about the mechanism.
did: They selected questions with explicit criteria (judges fail, debaters succeed, one clear right answer, no simple knock-down argument) and dropped problematic ones like the slinky question.
alternatives_named: text-based question-answering with limited quotes
questions requiring formal mathematical working
the slinky question
stated_reason: They want 'the easiest thing that should work but doesn't' to isolate where exactly the problems are, and don't expect debate to work when explanations are only empirical evidence.
quote: Generally, we want to find questions that are ‘the easiest thing that should work but doesn’t’ - this helps us isolate where exactly the problems are.
title: Writeup: Progress on AI Safety via Debate

problem: How to address the ambiguity exploited by dishonest debaters, given that rigid structures such as commitment and recursion left wiggle room.
did: They introduced cross-examination of non-communicating copies of the opposing debater, whose quotes can be exhibited to show inconsistency.
alternatives_named: formal argumentation styles
precommitment
recursive structures
asking for clarification in the main debate
stated_reason: It forces the dishonest debater to commit to details up front or answer inconsistently, and it happens outside the main thread so it doesn't consume judge attention.
quote: This forces the dishonest debater to either commit to all the details of their argument ahead of time (in which case the honest debater can focus on the flaw), or to answer questions inconsistently (in which case the honest debater can exhibit this inconsistency to the judge).
title: Writeup: Progress on AI Safety via Debate

problem: How strongly to claim that cross-examination solves the ambiguity problem.
did: They hedged: they expressed hope and offered a hand-wavy argument and a theory result, while acknowledging a dishonest strategy might still break it.
stated_reason: The argument is hand-wavy, and an evasive-yet-inconsistent dishonest strategy might defeat the mechanism.
quote: Overall, we’re hopeful that cross-examination will be helpful, but it seems possible that there’s a dishonest strategy that breaks it, likely involving some amount of evasion and inconsistency.
title: Writeup: Progress on AI Safety via Debate

problem: How the judge should evaluate debates, given that weighing the overall strength of arguments is hard and dishonest play is possible.
did: They instructed the judge to assume at least one debater is perfectly honest, so evidence of a lie means that debater loses, rather than weighing argument strength.
alternatives_named: weighing the overall strength of each debater’s arguments
stated_reason: Detecting evidence of a lie is a much easier task than weighing overall argument strength, and honest optimal play only requires the judge to prefer honesty over 50% of the time.
quote: This is in contrast to trying to weigh the overall strength of each debater’s arguments, which can be a much harder task than trying to detect evidence of a lie.
title: Writeup: Progress on AI Safety via Debate

problem: How to interpret the Bernoulli principle example where the honest debater believed an argument was wrong but couldn't locate the flaw.
did: They treated it as an example of the long computation problem and rejected the fix of relying on a simpler, more compelling overall argument (perpetual motion).
alternatives_named: relying on the simpler perpetual motion argument to let the honest debater win
stated_reason: Debate should let judges resolve based on the correctness of a very small claim rather than assessing the overall strength of two large arguments, which seems likelier to scale to domains the judge doesn't understand.
quote: In this case one might hope that the perpetual motion argument is simpler and more compelling and this would allow the honest debater to win. However, we want debate to allow judges to zoom in on particular parts of a debater’s argument
title: Writeup: Progress on AI Safety via Debate

problem: How to test whether the debate protocol works for verifying claims when real ML debaters are unavailable.
did: They ran debates with human judges and human debaters on physics questions, iteratively improving the mechanism.
quote: We tested the debate protocol introduced in [AI Safety via Debate](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.00899) with human judges and debaters. We found various problems and improved the mechanism to fix these issues (details of these are in the appendix).
title: Debate update: Obfuscated arguments problem

problem: Whether the obfuscated argument problem can be fixed or must be accepted as a limitation of the debate mechanism.
did: They concluded they have no fix and treat it as a potentially important quantitative limitation for both IDA and Debate.
stated_reason: Dishonest debaters can often build arguments with a fatal error that is very hard to locate.
quote: We don’t have a fix for this “obfuscated argument” problem, and believe it might be an important quantitative limitation for *both* IDA and Debate.
title: Debate update: Obfuscated arguments problem

problem: How to interpret the cryptographic RSA-2048 example, which is a simplified illustration of the problem.
did: They presented it as a simplistic illustration and explicitly noted it would not actually be a problem for debate, since honest and dishonest arguments look qualitatively different.
alternatives_named: taboo dishonest arguments of this flavor
stated_reason: The honest debater might convince the judge that the primality proof is easier than factoring, so absence of evidence is evidence of absence in their proof only.
quote: In this example, the honest and dishonest arguments look very qualitatively different. The honest debater might be able to convince the judge that the primality test proof is much easier than the factoring problem
title: Debate update: Obfuscated arguments problem

problem: Whether obfuscated dishonest arguments are distinguishable from honest arguments in practice.
did: They examined candidate distinguishing features (mismatch with the debater's actual reasoning, length and conjunctiveness) and compared partial honest trees against dishonest trees.
alternatives_named: differing from the debater's actual reasoning
being long, complicated and conjunctive
stated_reason: Honest debaters may also need arguments that do not mirror their reasoning, and honest arguments can also be long and conjunctive.
quote: Another possible distinction is that these arguments are long, complicated, and conjunctive. Unfortunately, the honest arguments can also end up being long and relatively conjunctive - an error in any one of a large number of nodes could undermine the whole argument.
title: Debate update: Obfuscated arguments problem

problem: How strongly to claim novelty for the obfuscated argument problem relative to earlier known issues with computationally intractable optimal play.
did: They credited earlier work and limited their claim to the observation that human natural-language debates let a dishonest debater construct such situations indistinguishably from honest play.
stated_reason: Geoffrey Irving and others had raised the general problem of intractable optimal play years earlier.
quote: The only new thing we’re presenting here is the observation that, in natural-language human debates, a dishonest debater can frequently construct such situations in a way that seems hard to distinguish from honest play.
title: Debate update: Obfuscated arguments problem

problem: Whether obfuscated arguments are only an artifact of the structured debate mechanism.
did: They checked for the same tactic in unstructured free-text debates, including explainer-vs-questioner and fully free-text formats.
stated_reason: To show the arguments can sow confusion even without the structured mechanism, though their usefulness to the dishonest debater is less clear there.
quote: These arguments are not just an artifact of our structured debate mechanism - they can also be used to sow confusion in a non-structured debate setting.
title: Debate update: Obfuscated arguments problem

problem: Whether to continue investigating this problem with human debate experiments or shift to other approaches.
did: They proposed moving toward approaches like learning the prior, judged better studied via ML experiments or theory than human experiments.
alternatives_named: finding a restricted class of arguments for which debaters can reliably find flaws
human experiments
stated_reason: Many important decisions cannot be justified with arguments small or robust enough to verify via debate, so trusting learned representations may be needed.
quote: We have been thinking about approaches like [learning the prior](/api/post/SL9mKhgdmDKXmxwE4) to help trust our models’ generalization. This is probably better investigated through ML experiments or theoretical research than through human experiments.
title: Debate update: Obfuscated arguments problem

problem: How to ensure judge quality in human debate experiments given low-quality judgements from crowdworkers.
did: They built a screening test for attentiveness and critical reasoning plus an easy physics quiz, accepting judges who got all reasoning questions right but missed at least one easy physics problem.
stated_reason: Positly judges gave low-quality judgements from inattentiveness or poor critical reasoning, and physics problems needed to remain hard for judges.
quote: We accepted judges who got 5/5 critical reasoning questions correct and at least one of the easy physics problems wrong.
title: Debate update: Obfuscated arguments problem

problem: How to get models to generalize from human-answerable questions to the questions we care about without defaulting to human-like answers.
did: They propose Imitative Generalisation, using ML only for IID imitation tasks while humans supervise how the transfer from D to D' is done via an optimised z.
alternatives_named: naive approach of fitting a model to D and running it on D'
hoping models naturally generalize correctly from easy-to-answer questions
stated_reason: Natural generalisation may be pathologically human-like, and IG avoids this by only using ML for IID tasks and imitating how humans generalize.
quote: It avoids the pathological generalisation by only using ML for IID tasks, and imitating the way humans generalize.
title: Imitative Generalisation (AKA 'Learning the Prior')

problem: How to get human judgments of prior and likelihood for training the models M^prior and M^L.
did: They ask labellers to compare pairs of z's or d's and use that as a reward signal rather than eliciting probabilities directly.
alternatives_named: asking humans to directly report P(z) or P(d|z)
stated_reason: Asking humans to directly report probabilities is unreasonable, and comparisons are easier for labellers.
quote: Asking humans to directly report $P(z)$or $P(d|z)$ is unreasonable. To make it easier for our labellers, we instead just ask them to compare pairs of $d$s or $z$s
title: Imitative Generalisation (AKA 'Learning the Prior')

problem: How to represent z so it captures what an NN could learn, is easy to optimise, and is human-understandable.
did: They consider a neural network plus text annotations as an alternative to pure text, with the NN initialised by training on D.
alternatives_named: z as a long string of natural-language text
stated_reason: Parts of the problem can be left as black boxes, the text can be shorter, and jointly optimising NN and annotations is likely easier than optimising a long text.
quote: It seems likely to be easier to jointly optimise a NN together with text annotations, than to optimise a long text that contains all of the information encoded in the NN weights.
