title: ARC Evals new report: Evaluating Language-Model Agents on Realistic Autonomous Tasks

problem: Whether to include the earlier TaskRabbit experiment in the report.
did: They excluded the TaskRabbit experiment from this report, pointing readers to a separate document.
stated_reason: It came from earlier iterations of the methodology and received more attention than anticipated.
quote: This experiment was not part of this report, but interested readers may learn more about it
title: ARC Evals new report: Evaluating Language-Model Agents on Realistic Autonomous Tasks

problem: Which kinds of tasks should be collected first to measure autonomous agent capability across a useful range of difficulty.
did: They chose to prioritize collecting harder tasks first, planning to derive easier variants from them by adding guidance or reducing requirements.
alternatives_named: collecting easier tasks first
shorter tasks
stated_reason: Easier variants of hard tasks can be made fairly straightforwardly, whereas hard tasks are the scarce, more informative resource.
quote: We're most interested in collecting harder tasks first, and we think we can often make easier variants of hard tasks quite straightforwardly - by providing more guidance or partial implementation of the task, or by reducing the requirements.
title: Bounty: Diverse hard tasks for LLM agents

problem: How to score agent performance on tasks so that scores are reliable and give signal across a range of ability.
did: They require continuous 0-1 scores, preferring automatic scoring but accepting robust manual rubrics over unreliable auto-scoring, and favoring non-binary scoring.
alternatives_named: unreliable automatic scoring function
binary scoring
multiple variants with different difficulty levels
stated_reason: Scores should reflect real ability and track difficulty rather than reflecting noise or formatting errors.
quote: Ideally tasks are automatically scorable, though we would strongly prefer a robust manually scored rubric over an unreliable auto scoring function Failing that, it should be as quick as possible for a human to score the task.
title: Bounty: Diverse hard tasks for LLM agents

problem: How to make sure agent success or failure on a task reflects real ability rather than bugs, shortcuts, or ambiguity.
did: They require a QA run-through by someone other than the task author, with detailed documentation of the run and of possible problems.
alternatives_named: author-only testing
stated_reason: Agents may succeed or fail for unexpected reasons such as scoring bugs, ambiguous instructions, missing resources, or shortcuts.
quote: In particular, you need to have somebody else run through the task to do quality assurance - making sure that the instructions aren't ambiguous, all the necessary resources are actually present, there isn't an accidental shortcut, etc.
title: Bounty: Diverse hard tasks for LLM agents

problem: Whether a task can be trusted as a measure given the possibility that current or future models have memorized its solution.
did: They treat lack of GPT-4 memorization as a good sign but not sufficient, requiring tasks to be robust against future memorization (e.g. solutions removed or filterable).
alternatives_named: accepting a task once GPT-4 hasn't memorized the solution
stated_reason: Future models might have memorized public solutions in more detail, so current non-memorization doesn't remove the concern.
quote: That's a good sign, but doesn't totally remove the memorization concern - we ideally want the tasks to be future-proof against models that might have memorized public solutions in more detail.
title: Bounty: Diverse hard tasks for LLM agents

problem: How to design the task suite's difficulty distribution so that capability trends can be extrapolated.
did: They aim for a fairly uniform distribution of task difficulty spanning a wide range rather than a bimodal one.
alternatives_named: bimodal distribution of difficulty
stated_reason: A uniform distribution lets them meaningfully extrapolate gradual increases in task success instead of seeing rapid progress, stalls, then rapid progress again.
quote: We also want the distribution of task difficulty to be fairly uniform, such that we can meaningfully extrapolate gradual increases in task success (as opposed to e.g. a bimodal distribution of difficulty
title: Bounty: Diverse hard tasks for LLM agents

problem: Whether to build tasks around specific threat models or around general capabilities.
did: They focus on general capabilities, treating specific threat-model information as a bonus.
alternatives_named: ruling out specific threat stories
stated_reason: It seems hard to rule out danger from a broadly capable agent just by ruling out specific threat stories.
quote: But we're focusing on the general capabilities because it seems hard to rule out danger from an agent that's able to carry out a wide variety of multi-day expert-level projects
title: Bounty: Diverse hard tasks for LLM agents

problem: How to avoid the task suite having a shared bottleneck that would cause sudden jumps in measured performance.
did: They require diversity of bottlenecks, so agents get stuck in different ways on different tasks.
alternatives_named: tasks all blocked on browsing, authentication, or ML knowledge
stated_reason: A shared bottleneck could produce a sudden big jump in task performance after a small improvement to the agent.
quote: We want agents to get stuck in different ways on the different tasks - we don't want it to be the case that all of the tasks are blocked on browsing, or authentication, or ML knowledge or something
title: Bounty: Diverse hard tasks for LLM agents

problem: Whether tasks should include restrictions, such as limited internet access, to control difficulty and contamination.
did: They allow offline or archived resources for static difficulty but forbid artificial restrictions not applicable to real-life threat models.
alternatives_named: making the task harder with artificial restrictions
general internet access
stated_reason: An actual ARA agent would be able to use the internet and run code, so artificial restrictions would not match real-life threat models.
quote: No artificial restrictions: don't make the task harder in ways that aren't applicable to the real-life threat models - an actual ARA agent would be able to use the internet, run code, etc.
title: Bounty: Diverse hard tasks for LLM agents

problem: Whether METR should prioritize developing evaluation science or becoming an auditor of frontier models.
did: METR made developing the science of evaluations its top priority and treated becoming an auditor as unnecessary for that goal.
alternatives_named: becoming an auditor
stated_reason: METR does not need to be an auditor in order to succeed at developing the science of evaluations.
quote: METR’s top priority is to develop the science of evaluations, and we don’t need to be auditors in order to succeed at this.
title: Clarifying METR's Auditing Role

problem: How to design evaluation protocols so they are useful regardless of who runs the evaluation.
did: METR aims to build evaluation protocols that any evaluator can use, including governments, internal lab teams, other third parties or METR itself.
alternatives_named: government
an internal lab team
another third party
a team at METR
quote: We aim to build evaluation protocols that can be used by evaluators/auditors regardless of whether that is the government, an internal lab team, another third party, or a team at METR.
title: Clarifying METR's Auditing Role

problem: How to characterize METR's earlier work on GPT-4 and Claude, given confusion over whether those were audits.
did: METR characterized the earlier work as informal pilots or research collaborations rather than audits.
alternatives_named: audit
stated_reason: The work did not provide meaningful oversight.
quote: Those were informal pilots of what an audit might involve, or research collaborations – not providing meaningful oversight.
title: Clarifying METR's Auditing Role

problem: How strongly to claim that the earlier pre-deployment work amounted to oversight or accountability.
did: METR declined to claim it had audited the models, pointing to the NDA terms and the absence of any formal link to deployment decisions.
stated_reason: Under the NDA METR had no right or responsibility to disclose findings, and no formal expectation existed that the work would inform deployment decisions.
quote: it was all under NDA – we didn’t have any right or responsibility to disclose our findings to anyone outside the labs – and there wasn’t any formal expectation it would inform deployment decisions.
title: Clarifying METR's Auditing Role

problem: Whether results from the early-access GPT-4 evaluation could be accepted as a reliable judgment of risky capabilities.
did: METR cited the system card's statement that the results were not reliable without testing the final model and doing its own fine-tuning.
alternatives_named: evaluating only early model versions without fine-tuning
stated_reason: The evaluators lacked access to the final model and could not fine-tune it, and the final version had capability improvements that could change performance.
quote: As a next step, ARC will need to conduct experiments that (a) involve the final version of the deployed model (b) involve ARC doing its own fine-tuning, before a reliable judgment of the risky emergent capabilities of GPT-4-launch can be made
title: Clarifying METR's Auditing Role

problem: What access arrangements are needed for third-party evaluation to be meaningful.
did: METR called for third-party evaluators to have formal arrangements and access commitments, both before scaling or deployment and for evaluation research.
alternatives_named: informal pilot procedures
non-public access without formal commitments
stated_reason: Formal arrangements are needed to evaluate new frontier models before they are scaled up or deployed and to conduct research to improve evaluations.
quote: We think it’s important for there to be third-party evaluators with formal arrangements and access commitments - both for evaluating new frontier models before they are scaled up or deployed, and for conducting research to improve evaluations.
title: Clarifying METR's Auditing Role

problem: Whether METR should expand into conducting third-party evaluations itself.
did: METR stated it is interested and may hire and fundraise, but made expansion conditional on external factors and open to other actors entering the space.
alternatives_named: other actors entering the space
governments conducting audits in-house
stated_reason: Expansion depends on whether governments mandate access, whether labs give access, hiring success, and whether it detracts from developing the science.
quote: We are interested in conducting third-party evaluations and may hire & fundraise to do so, but would also be happy to see other actors enter the space.
title: Clarifying METR's Auditing Role

problem: How to evaluate whether AI can cause catastrophic harm, given uncertainty about which specific cognitive capabilities are limiting.
did: They chose end-to-end, threat-model-driven task evaluations built as a chain from real-world threat to measurable proxies, rather than measuring isolated cognitive abilities.
alternatives_named: directly identifying the key missing cognitive capability and measuring that
generic ML benchmarks
academic fine-grained questions about specific reasoning
stated_reason: It is hard to know the limiting capabilities, and going straight to a particular dimension risks it not being linked to the real-world outcomes of concern; benchmarks also saturate quickly and are poor proxies for models.
quote: But I think we do actually want to work backwards from something that we think is a better proxy for danger and see if we can distill that into some more specific underlying capability
title: 34 - AI Evaluations with Beth Barnes | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

problem: How to elicit model capabilities without fooling oneself that the evaluators' own prompt-engineering supplies the capability.
did: They advocate doing all elicitation on a dev set and evaluating on a separate test set, with generalization gap matching that between test set and the real-world target.
alternatives_named: task-specific elicitation on the evaluated tasks
IID split versus artificially adding distributional shift
stated_reason: Task-specific or narrowly targeted elicitation can put the answer in, so the held-out test keeps the evaluation fair.
quote: So the way we think you should actually do this is you do all your elicitation against a dev set and then you evaluate on a separate test set so it’s fair.
title: 34 - AI Evaluations with Beth Barnes | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

problem: How to interpret the GPT-4 evaluation results when the evaluators lacked fine-tuning access and the model failed at scary tasks.
did: They patched over problems they expected to be fixable soon (e.g., browsing via a human-simulated agent, reminders, hallucinated text) and treated continued failure as a soft upper bound with added margin.
alternatives_named: evaluating the model as-is without patching
using existing tools for blind users
stated_reason: Without patching, all tasks fail for the same reason, giving no information about what the next hurdle is; fixable limitations are likely to be removed soon.
quote: You don’t want to be in the situation where all of your tasks are failing for the same reason, that you think is a thing that might change quickly, because then you’re just not getting any information
title: 34 - AI Evaluations with Beth Barnes | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

problem: Whether current models might be deliberately sandbagging evaluations.
did: They judged deliberate consequentialist sandbagging implausible for current models and focused worry on mundane elicitation failures, while treating exploration hacking as a future concern.
alternatives_named: worrying about deliberate scheming sandbagging now
gradient hacking
stated_reason: Doing so would require advanced single-forward-pass reasoning beyond long chain-of-thought, implying implausible capability discontinuities.
quote: They’re not good enough. It just seems like they would have to be doing things in a single forward pass in a single token that are very advanced compared to what they can do in long chain of thought
title: 34 - AI Evaluations with Beth Barnes | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

problem: How to test whether a model is sandbagging or hiding capabilities when direct elicitation may fail.
did: They propose fine-tuning on human-like policies/supervised data to show the capability, assuming no gradient hacking, and distinguishing knowing the capabilities from knowing whether you know them.
alternatives_named: prompting alone
classification data set the model cannot fit as an upper bound
stated_reason: If the model can be fine-tuned to show the capability, you must assume it has it; this works unless the capability is too superhuman to have example data.
quote: Then if you assume they can’t gradient hack, then for anything on which you can construct a policy by which the model should be able to do the task, you can then just fine-tune it on that.
title: 34 - AI Evaluations with Beth Barnes | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

problem: How to structure red lines and buffers so evaluations give warning before dangerous capability levels.
did: They emphasized building a smooth y-axis of dangerous capability and either setting a red line then adjusting down by a buffer, or building the furthest-out eval confidently preceding the risk.
alternatives_named: create the red line then adjust down for buffer
create the furthest-out eval that still clearly comes before the risk
modify tasks or agent assistance to define the buffer gap
stated_reason: The bottleneck to scaling-law extrapolation is a good y-axis whose increments mean the same thing; random benchmark scaling laws don't relate to risk.
quote: There’s two ways you could think about it: one is first, you create the red line and then you figure out how much buffer, you adjust down from that.
title: 34 - AI Evaluations with Beth Barnes | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

problem: How to design lab policy commitments: prescriptive mitigations versus lab-specific red lines.
did: They shifted from prescriptive, situation-specific mitigation requirements to letting each lab set its own red lines with general pressure to improve them.
alternatives_named: prescriptive mitigations per situation
complicated conditionals
safety case with review process
stated_reason: Labs differ in situations and costs, and uncertain capability profiles meant prescriptive rules were either overly complex or overly conservative.
quote: So that’s why we ended up going to more [towards] each lab can say what their red lines are and then there’s some general pressure and ratchet to hopefully make those better.
title: 34 - AI Evaluations with Beth Barnes | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

problem: Whether to continue building a classification data set that upper-bounds model capability.
did: They tried creating a classification dataset capturing hard parts of tasks but moved on to other work because it was hard.
stated_reason: It was hard, though it would give stronger guarantees about the model not being able to do the task.
quote: And in particular, something that we tried to do for a while, but ended up moving on to other things, which was hard, was creating a classification data set that captures the hard parts of doing a particular task
title: 34 - AI Evaluations with Beth Barnes | AXRP - the AI X-risk Research Podcast

problem: How to make an early-warning AI R&D evaluation interpretable and grounded in terms of automation risk.
did: They compared AI agents directly to human experts under equivalent conditions and resources, using 8-hour human baselines on seven environments.
alternatives_named: benchmarks without human comparisons
human comparisons under different conditions (e.g., Kaggle participants in MLE-bench)
short-horizon QA-style human comparisons
stated_reason: Equivalent-condition human comparisons give a clear logical link to automation risk and help confirm feasibility and ground the interpretation of agent results.
quote: In this work, we present RE-Bench, which aims to evaluate whether AI agents can fully automate the work of expert AI R&D researchers, using direct performance comparisons between AI agents and human experts under equivalent conditions and resources.
title: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts

problem: How to establish that the environments are feasible and not saturated, so that low agent scores are meaningful.
did: They validated each environment with four metrics: expert progress, expert-reported score matching expectation, variance of starting score, and major technical issues, plus an informal estimate of expert saturation.
stated_reason: Ensuring human experts reliably make progress provides assurance that environments are feasible and have unambiguous instructions, and a high ceiling prevents saturation.
quote: To assess our second design pillar (that human experts reliably make progress and avoid issues, while not saturating the environments by running into a score ceiling), we investigated 4 metrics.
title: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts

problem: How to compare agents against humans given large variance across human attempts and sources.
did: They cautioned against comparing to the average human result and argued that comparison to the most successful human attempts is more suitable.
alternatives_named: comparing against the average human result
stated_reason: Human results vary widely, and different baseliner sources differ significantly (0.96 vs 0.46 average), while the risk question concerns researchers at their best.
quote: Because of the high variance of human results, and the significant differences between baseliners from different sources, we caution against narrowly focusing AI agent comparisons on the average human result.
title: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts

problem: How to give agents and humans equal resources, and how to limit agent runs.
did: They limited agents by wall-clock time rather than token usage, so agents and humans get equal GPU hours, and did not count API errors or rate-limit pauses.
alternatives_named: token usage limit
stated_reason: It makes sure agents and humans are given an equal amount of GPU hours, and API latency has only a modest effect since agents mostly wait for computations.
quote: Similar to MLE-bench [25], we ran the agent with a wall-clock time limit, rather than a token usage limit, to make sure that agents and humans are given an equal amount of GPU hours with which to complete experiments
title: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts

problem: How to compare agents and humans fairly across different time budgets, given agents' strategies differ.
did: They evaluated best-of-k with multiple allocations of a fixed total time budget (e.g., 30-minute vs 2-hour vs 8-hour runs) and used the best allocation per agent for the headline comparison.
alternatives_named: a single long run
other time horizons such as 16 hours per attempt for humans or 8-hour attempts for agents
stated_reason: Best-of-k resets could be implemented by agents themselves by resetting environment and context, so it is considered a fair comparison.
quote: Note that this is a procedure which AI agents could implement themselves by regularly resetting their environment and deleting their context, and so we believe this is a fair comparison.
title: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts

problem: How to interpret the best agent score on the noisy Finetune GPT-2 for QA environment.
did: They reran the best agent solution, found its score dropped from 0.88 to 0.69, and concluded the original result was partly overfitting to noise, so the environment likely underestimates the human-AI gap.
stated_reason: The rerun score was significantly lower than the original, indicating the high score was partially driven by noise.
quote: Rerunning the agent solution, it achieves a normalized score of only 0.69 (significantly lower than the original score of 0.88), indicating that the high agent score is partially driven by overfitting to this noise.
title: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts

problem: How to check that high-scoring agent runs are legitimate rather than exploiting loopholes, given that manual inspection of all runs was infeasible.
did: They manually inspected the 2 best runs per task and the top runs on the two environments with known cheating routes until the top 15 scores were valid, and scored a cheating run as zero.
alternatives_named: manually inspecting all agent runs
stated_reason: Those two environments are the only ones where the authors know of simple ways to cheat.
quote: We were not able to inspect all agent runs manually, instead we only carefully inspected the 2 best performing runs of each task, and inspected the top performing runs on ‘Restricted Architecture MLM’ and ‘Optimize LLM Foundry’ until we knew that the top 15 scores were all valid
title: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts

problem: How strongly to claim that RE-Bench results reflect real-world AI R&D automation capability.
did: They stated that the real human-AI gap is likely much larger than observed, and that agents matching humans here may still be far from automating AI R&D, while also noting factors that could cause underestimation.
stated_reason: Real AI R&D is at least 2 orders of magnitude larger in scale across many dimensions, and RE-Bench tasks are cleanly defined and non-interacting.
quote: We expect the human–AI gap in real-world AI R&D to be much larger than the gap observed on these evaluations, and find it fairly plausible that the first agents that match top human performance in these environments may still be far from capable of AI R&D automation.
title: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts

problem: Whether to keep candidate environments during benchmark construction when they performed poorly on design criteria.
did: They iterated through three stages (specification, implementation, baselining) and dropped many specifications and completed implementations that performed poorly.
stated_reason: Environments needed to meet the feasibility and saturation-resistance pillars; baselining often showed problems requiring major adjustments or dropping.
quote: Each environment is the product of significant iteration, and in the process of developing these 7, we dropped over 12 specifications (at various levels of completion), and more than 5 completed implementations which encountered unexpected difficulties or performed poorly on our criteria.
title: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts

problem: How to establish a fair, grounded comparison of human and AI task difficulty so time estimates reflect real work.
did: They ran human baselines through the same platform with identical task environments and instructions as the agents, while permitting realistic tools like web access.
alternatives_named: informal time estimates
comparing human and AI performance under very different conditions (compute, knowledge of modern methods, wall-clock time)
stated_reason: They want a fair comparison between agents and humans while giving humans realistic affordances so baseline times represent normal work productivity.
quote: Both humans and agents are therefore provided with an identical task environment, identical task instructions—humans receive setup instructions, but no additional task-specific information beyond what agents receive, and a comparable task interface
title: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks

problem: How to verify that tasks are valid, i.e. that agent successes and failures reflect real capability rather than bugs or reward hacking.
did: They had an AI agent attempt every task five times and manually read all 945 transcripts to check successes were legitimate and failures were not due to environment problems.
alternatives_named: human QA runs alone
stated_reason: Manual transcript review surfaces silent and explicit bugs in task code that human quality assurance attempts did not detect.
quote: Finally, we have an AI agent (typically Claude 3.5 Sonnet (new), although other models were sometimes used) attempt every task five times. We then manually read through each of the 945 resulting transcripts.
title: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks

problem: What time estimate to assign to tasks for which no baseliner succeeded.
did: They used the geometric mean of successful baseline times, and fell back on forecasts from the task creator or a familiar author for tasks with no successful baselines.
alternatives_named: collecting baselines for all tasks
stated_reason: Budget and time limits and logistical challenges with long tasks prevented baselines for 50 tasks, and 29 more had only failed attempts.
quote: The time estimate for a task is the (geometric) mean of successful baseline times. For tasks with no successful baselines, we use a forecast from the task creator or an author familiar with the task
title: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks

problem: How much to trust informal forecasts as a substitute for baselines, given that 79 tasks rely on them.
did: They compared forecasts to successful baseline times, found R^2=0.51, and concluded forecasts are a reasonable proxy but that baselines still add substantial information.
stated_reason: The moderate correlation indicates forecasts are informative but leave considerable unexplained variance.
quote: The correlation coefficient is $R^{2}=0.51$, indicating that our informal estimates are a reasonable proxy for the actual baseline times, but that we still get a substantial amount of information from collecting baselines.
title: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks

problem: Whether baseliners should be allowed internet access when some tasks could be trivialized by external resources.
did: They always permitted web access to baseliners but banned AI assistants, Wolfram Alpha, and sign-in services.
alternatives_named: restricting internet access for baseliners
stated_reason: Pilot studies showed significantly reduced human performance without web access, often from small hindrances like forgetting syntax.
quote: However, pilot studies revealed significantly reduced human baseline performance without web access, often due to small hindrances such as forgetting programming language syntax. Consequently, baseline participants are always permitted external web access.
title: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks

problem: How to design baseliner incentives so time estimates reflect efficient task completion rather than excessive checking.
did: They added a speed bonus for the fastest successful baseliner, in addition to a success bonus weighted by average task time.
alternatives_named: hourly wage only
stated_reason: In an early pilot, some baseliners spent many hours re-checking solutions, so the bonus pushes estimates toward lower-bounding human time.
quote: In an early pilot, some baseliners spent many hours checking and re-checking their solutions, to marginally increase the probability that their solution was correct. To prevent this, and to broadly push our task time estimates towards lower-bounding the time for humans
title: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks

problem: Whether to accept baselines collected early without the incentive scheme.
did: They kept the early wage-only baselines in the dataset.
alternatives_named: excluding baselines collected without incentives
stated_reason: They provide valuable data, are relatively few, and the resulting time estimates appear qualitatively reasonable.
quote: A small number of early baselines were collected without these incentives, compensating baseliners solely through an hourly wage. We include these baselines because they still provide valuable data, there are a relatively small number of them
title: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks

problem: Whether agent results are sensitive to analysis choices such as binarizing scores or uneven task-family sizes.
did: They ran ablations using average continuous scores instead of binarized success, and a family-size weighted average using the inverse square root of family size.
alternatives_named: binarizing via success thresholds
unweighted averaging across tasks
stated_reason: Task families with more tasks might bias or skew results, and continuous scores give higher resolution signal.
quote: Because tasks are grouped into task families, one concern might be that results are biased or skewed by task families that have more tasks than other families. To evaluate whether this is the case, Figure 9 and Figure 10 present results
title: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks

problem: How strongly to claim that measured agent performance reflects the models' true capabilities.
did: They framed the agent results as a reasonable lower bound and noted that better prompting and scaffolding would likely improve performance.
stated_reason: Agent scaffolds were not heavily optimized, so full capabilities of frontier models remain undetermined.
quote: We believe our agent results are a reasonable lower bound, but better prompting and scaffolding is likely to improve performance. Future work will be necessary to determine the full capabilities of current frontier models.
title: HCAST: Human-Calibrated Autonomy Software Tasks

problem: How to measure AI capabilities on a scale that is meaningful in the real world and not decoupled from real utility, as benchmarks and qualitative impressions are.
did: METR built a diverse suite of autonomy-requiring tasks, had skilled humans attempt nearly all of them, and used human completion time as the Y-axis for the model's 50% success point.
alternatives_named: qualitative impressions of model usefulness
saturating standard benchmarks like coding competition problems
stated_reason: Qualitative impressions can't be turned into a trend, and benchmarks tend to be decoupled from real-world usefulness; diverse tasks are harder to overfit to.
quote: So we’ve been building this suite of diverse autonomy-requiring tasks, where the model has basically access to a computer and it can do stuff on the computer and use tools and run code and do whatever to accomplish the task.
title: #217 – Beth Barnes on the most important graph in AI right now — and the 7-month rule that governs its progress - 80,000 Hours Podcast

problem: How to get a fair measure of model capabilities on tasks, avoiding spurious failures that understate what models can do.
did: METR had humans actually attempt the tasks to remove ambiguous or broken tasks, and spent substantial elicitation effort and compute giving models resources comparable to what a human would cost.
alternatives_named: contractors judging task difficulty without attempting it (as in SWE-bench Verified)
typical cheap per-query model spend
stated_reason: Having humans do the tasks removes spurious failures, and it would be bad to conclude models are incapable when they're capable and merely cheaper than humans.
quote: So we tried hard to give the model fair resources and benchmark it fairly against humans and have reasonable spend compared to what it would cost for a human.
title: #217 – Beth Barnes on the most important graph in AI right now — and the 7-month rule that governs its progress - 80,000 Hours Podcast

problem: How much to trust the headline doubling-time estimate for task horizon, given noise and methodological choices.
did: METR ran a sensitivity analysis over data noise and methodological choices, reported a range of doubling times rather than a point estimate, and applied a mental correction for eval-friendly tasks being easier than real tasks.
alternatives_named: reporting a single six-month doubling time
stated_reason: Tasks that make good automatically scorable evals may be systematically easier for models, so absolute horizons may overstate real-world ability, though the exponential trend is solid.
quote: we also did a sort of ablation [sensitivity analysis] both over the actual noise in the data and over different methodological choices we could make, and the range of estimates you get is basically between three months and one year.
title: #217 – Beth Barnes on the most important graph in AI right now — and the 7-month rule that governs its progress - 80,000 Hours Podcast

problem: How to evaluate whether a model is dangerous when it could be sandbagging or reasoning about being evaluated, and when evals are run on a safeguarded model.
did: Beth argues evals should measure maximum easily reachable capabilities of the pre-mitigation model, including cheap fine-tuning or better scaffolding, rather than only the deployed, safeguarded configuration.
alternatives_named: evaluating only the model as deployed with mitigations and safeguards
evaluating with weak agent scaffolding
stated_reason: Models can be stolen, misused internally, or fine-tuned, so what matters is how dangerous the model could be without the deployment safeguards.
quote: So when you’re doing these kinds of evals, you really want to be like, what are the maximum easily reachable capabilities of this model? This is the idea of “pre-mitigation” — as opposed to once you’ve trained it to refuse various things
title: #217 – Beth Barnes on the most important graph in AI right now — and the 7-month rule that governs its progress - 80,000 Hours Podcast

problem: At what stage of the model lifecycle should safety evaluation be focused.
did: Beth argues for prioritising evaluations before and during large training runs and before internal deployment, rather than the dominant pre-deployment-to-the-public framing.
alternatives_named: pre-deployment testing before public API release
one giant training run followed by evaluation
stated_reason: After a costly model exists it is hard not to use it, it can be stolen or misused internally, and public deployment is relatively reversible whereas internal capability buildup has no outside oversight.
quote: In general the most emphasis has been on this idea of pre-deployment testing: before you start serving this model on your API to the general public, you do some testing in house
title: #217 – Beth Barnes on the most important graph in AI right now — and the 7-month rule that governs its progress - 80,000 Hours Podcast

problem: How strongly to state timeline claims about recursive self-improvement given caveats on the measured horizon and doubling time.
did: Beth endorses that two years wouldn't be surprising and frames the standard as needing confidence it won't happen, not confidence it will, while acknowledging caveats.
alternatives_named: waiting for high confidence before acting
stated_reason: Even a roughly 1% chance of takeover risk is high stakes for currently living people, so whole-number-percent risks warrant concern.

problem: How to interpret the paper's finding that the AD transformer improves in-context on held-out Dark Room tasks, which could indicate a general RL algorithm or a simpler mechanism.

problem: How to judge whether the training and deployment tasks in the paper are genuinely different, which determines whether generalization to them demonstrates a general algorithm.
did: Argued that tasks differing only in goal location should not count as different under a reasonable notion of task.

quote: If the AD agent trained in this paper were able to learn to do any non-trivially different task (e.g. an AD agent trained on Dark Room tasks were able to in-context learn a task involving collecting keys and unlocking boxes), then I would take that as strong evidence
title: Caution when interpreting Deepmind's In-context RL paper

problem: How to interpret the authors' explanation that ED fails because it cannot explore while AD can.

problem: How strongly to state the claim about what the AD agents actually learned, given the lack of direct verification.
did: Hedged the claim with phrases like 'strongly suspect' and conceded the agent may have learned a few additional heuristics, while still denying mesa-optimizer status.

title: Caution when interpreting Deepmind's In-context RL paper

problem: What the ED agents do at deployment given they fail to improve, with no direct data in the paper to settle it.

title: Caution when interpreting Deepmind's In-context RL paper

alternatives_named: measuring LLMs' capabilities for classifying the factuality of challenging data
complicated and structured, confusing, or intentionally misleading statements as in prior work

title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in LLM Representations of True/False Datasets

problem: How to rule out that probes detect probable vs. improbable text rather than truth.
did: They introduced a nonfactual 'likely' dataset and used negated datasets where truth and text probability are anti-correlated, to test probes against the probability confound.
stated_reason: To ensure the truth representations do not merely reflect a representation of probable vs. improbable text.
quote: To ensure that our truth representations do not merely reflect a representation of probable vs. improbable text, we introduce a likely dataset, consisting of nonfactual text where the final token is either the most or 100th most likely completion according to LLaMA-13B.

problem: Which hidden states to analyze for truth representations.
did: They used activation patching between true and false prompts to localize causally implicated hidden states, then studied the group (b) states over the end-of-statement punctuation.
stated_reason: The group (b) states encode information about the full statement and are causally influential on the TRUE/FALSE output, so they hypothesize they store the statement's truth.
quote: Since the information encoded is also causally influential on the model’s decision to output “TRUE” or “FALSE,” we hypothesize that these hidden states store a representation of the statement’s truth.
title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in LLM Representations of True/False Datasets

stated_reason: This lets them measure increased data diversity in a particular way by mitigating features with opposite-sign correlations with truth.
quote: By comparing probes trained on cities to probes trained on cities + neg_cities, we are able to measure the effect of increasing data diversity in a particular, targeted way
title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in LLM Representations of True/False Datasets

problem: Whether probe classification accuracy suffices to show a probe finds the direction the model uses.

alternatives_named: evaluating interventions only in-distribution as in prior work (Li et al., 2023b)

quote: Our goal is to cause LLMs to treat false statements appearing in context as true and vice versa. Crucially—and in contrast to prior work (Li et al., 2023b)—we evaluate our interventions on OOD inputs.
title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in LLM Representations of True/False Datasets

problem: How to interpret misaligned truth axes across datasets (e.g., cities vs. neg_cities) in PCA visualizations.

quote: If so, we would expect training linear probes on $\mathcal{D}\cup\mathcal{D}^{\prime}$ to result in improved generalization, despite $\mathcal{D}^{\prime}$ consisting of the same statements as $\mathcal{D}$, but with the word “not” inserted.
title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in LLM Representations of True/False Datasets

quote: The performance here may be due to the strong correlation ($r=.95$) between inputs being true and probable (according to LLaMA-2-70B) on sp_en_trans.
title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in LLM Representations of True/False Datasets

title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in LLM Representations of True/False Datasets

problem: Whether a skeptical prior about LLMs linearly representing XORs of arbitrary features is correct.

stated_reason: The author thought the claim was absurd in general and in the GDM paper's setting, so tested it directly.
quote: For reasons that I’ll explain below, I thought this claim was absolutely bonkers, both in general and in the specific setting that the GDM paper was working in. So I ran some experiments to prove Rohin wrong.

problem: Which dataset to use to test whether XORs are linearly represented.

alternatives_named: datasets from the CCS paper (also used by the CCS challenges paper)
stated_reason: The author considers the CCS datasets especially awful and the cities datasets quite good.
quote: For a while it has been my opinion that the datasets people use to study this stuff are bad, and that the datasets from the CCS paper (also used by the CCS challenges paper) are especially awful.
title: What’s up with LLMs representing XORs of arbitrary features?

problem: How to choose features so that finding an XOR probe is not explained by the XOR being a naturally useful feature.
did: Chose has_alice and has_not as arbitrary features lacking any natural interpretation for their XOR.
alternatives_named: cases where the xor of two features might have a natural meaning
stated_reason: The test only demonstrates RAX if the model has no plausible downstream use for the XOR.
quote: I’ll note that it’s very important to me that has\_alice xor has\_not doesn’t have any “natural interpretation” as a feature that the model would want to compute anyway (unlike other cases where the xor of two features might have a natural meaning).
title: What’s up with LLMs representing XORs of arbitrary features?

problem: Whether the XOR probe result depends on a particular dataset setup or probe design.
did: Ran variations: Alice/Bob appended at the end with a different token position, and random LLaMA generations with true/false and banana/shed features.
stated_reason: To check robustness of the XOR finding across setups.
quote: “Alice” or “Bob” were appended to the end instead of prepended, and the hidden state was extracted over the “Alice” / “Bob” token.
title: What’s up with LLMs representing XORs of arbitrary features?

problem: How to rule out that XOR probe accuracy comes from the linear separability of has_not itself.
did: Independently centered negated and unnegated statements by subtracting their means so has_not is not linearly decodable, then probed XORs.
stated_reason: This makes it impossible for a linear probe to get good accuracy on has_not, isolating the XOR representation.
quote: I’ll independently center the datasets of negated and unnegated statements by subtracting off their means. This will make it impossible for a linear probe to get good accuracy for the feature has\_not.
title: What’s up with LLMs representing XORs of arbitrary features?

problem: Whether XORs are represented merely incidentally because high-dimensional random-ish network computation can produce them by chance.
did: Reran the experiments on a 'reset' LLaMA-2-13B with weights shuffled along the last dimension, as a control.
alternatives_named: reinitializing the weights according to some distribution
stated_reason: Shuffling erases everything learned in training while maintaining basic statistical properties of the weights, so it is more principled.
quote: I reran my experiments from above on a “reset” version of LLaMA-2-13B. What this means is that, for each parameter in LLaMA-2-13B, I shuffled the weights of that parameter by permuting them along the last dimension
title: What’s up with LLMs representing XORs of arbitrary features?

problem: How to interpret the reset-network probe accuracy on the XOR feature given the baseline from linear probes on a simple OR heuristic.
did: Compared the probe against the 0.75 accuracy achievable by an 'or' probe and concluded XOR is not linearly represented in the reset model since the probe doesn't beat it.
stated_reason: Given linearly represented has_alice and has_not, an OR probe automatically reaches at least 0.75, so only exceeding it indicates a real XOR representation.
quote: Given that has\_alice and has\_not are linearly represented, a linear probe can automatically get at least .75 accuracy on “has\_alice xor has\_not” by being a “has_alice or has not” probe. The probe trained here does not beat that baseline.
title: What’s up with LLMs representing XORs of arbitrary features?

problem: How confidently to endorse an explanation for XOR representation when the evidence conflicts with it.
did: Judged the noisy-aggregation explanation surprising given perfect XOR probe accuracy, yet still gave it the most weight, and stated overall confusion.
alternatives_named: basic features are more salient by design
models track which features are basic
models compute some XORs in early layers
stated_reason: Perfect probe accuracy would require many correlated features or a few noise-free ones, which is surprising for random features, but other explanations seem worse.
quote: Nevertheless, I think this is currently the explanation that I put the most weight on.
title: What’s up with LLMs representing XORs of arbitrary features?

problem: Choosing how to approximate indirect effects of nodes, given that cheap attribution patching underestimates effects for some components.

title: Sparse Feature Circuits: Discovering and Editing Interpretable Causal Graphs in Language Models

problem: How strongly to claim the quality of the automatically discovered clusters and circuits, given no established way to evaluate them.

stated_reason: Evaluating clusters and circuits is an important open problem, so claims rest on qualitative impressions.
quote: While evaluating these clusters and circuits is an important open problem, we generally find that these clusters expose interesting LM behaviors, and that their respective feature circuits can provide useful insights on mechanisms of LM behavior.
title: Sparse Feature Circuits: Discovering and Editing Interpretable Causal Graphs in Language Models

problem: How to interpret the higher human interpretability ratings for sparse features, given that annotators were not a random sample of humans.

alternatives_named: a truly random sample of human annotators

problem: How to study the difficulty of discriminating good from bad models when existing scalable oversight approaches rely on judging outputs.
did: Imposed the pessimistic assumption that the models are behaviorally identical, forcing a focus on cognition-based oversight rather than improving output-based oversight.
alternatives_named: debate (justification-based oversight)
process-based oversight
discriminating models by their outputs
stated_reason: Assuming behavioral identity precludes input/output approaches and forces discrimination based on the models' cognition.
quote: Instead of asking how to improve the existing approaches to scalable oversight, I’m going to take a different tack: **I will impose the pessimistic assumption that our models are effectively** ***behaviorally identical***, i.e. that we’re not able to discriminate our models on the basis of their input/output behavior.
title: Discriminating Behaviorally Identical Classifiers: a model problem for applying interpretability to scalable oversight

problem: How to formulate a concrete, tractable problem that captures the technical difficulty of cognition-based oversight.
did: Simplified to a classification setting (DBIC) where model outputs can be exactly identical, rather than general agents or generative models.
alternatives_named: RL agents
generative models
stated_reason: The simplified problem is crisper and easier to articulate while still capturing most of the technical difficulty, and removes tricky assumptions about limits of overseer judgment.
quote: The main move here is to simplify the setting by assuming that our AI systems are *classifiers*, rather than more general AI systems like RL agents or generative models.
title: Discriminating Behaviorally Identical Classifiers: a model problem for applying interpretability to scalable oversight

problem: What data should a DBIC solver be allowed to access beyond the ambiguous subdistribution.
did: Distinguished Hard DBIC (no classification data outside D_a) from Relaxed DBIC (unlabeled inputs from outside D_a), and stated a preference for progress on the hard version.
alternatives_named: Relaxed DBIC
access to labeled data where classifiers disagree
stated_reason: It is unclear that lots of samples from D \ D_a will be available in practice.
quote: In practice, I’m not sure if we’ll be able to assume access to lots of samples from $D \setminus D_a$, so I’d prefer progress on hard DBIC to relaxed DBIC.
title: Discriminating Behaviorally Identical Classifiers: a model problem for applying interpretability to scalable oversight

problem: How to detect that a classifier trained on ambiguous data generalizes badly without access to balanced data.
did: Trained SAEs, identified the SAE features most causally implicated in the classifier's outputs on ambiguous data, and manually interpreted them for task-irrelevant (gender) features.
alternatives_named: evaluating on the balanced dataset

quote: Right now, the (somewhat sad) SoTA for understanding SAE features is “look for patterns in their top-activating contexts and most-promoted tokens.” Fortunately, that’s enough for this task; here are the Neuronpedia pages for some of the 67 features.
title: Discriminating Behaviorally Identical Classifiers: a model problem for applying interpretability to scalable oversight

problem: Whether the SHIFT experiment, which has only one classifier, legitimately demonstrates progress on DBIC as defined with a pair of classifiers.
did: Acknowledged the mismatch and judged it unimportant, arguing that lacking a benign reference classifier makes the task harder, then restated the workflow in strict DBIC form.
stated_reason: The lack of a benign reference classifier should make things harder, not easier, so success is not inflated by the difference.

title: Discriminating Behaviorally Identical Classifiers: a model problem for applying interpretability to scalable oversight

problem: How to validate and benchmark the SHIFT edits against meaningful comparisons.
did: Compared SHIFT to a Concept Bottleneck Probing baseline and to neuron/feature skylines that cheat by using the balanced set, plus an oracle classifier trained on balanced data.
alternatives_named: Concept Bottleneck Probing
neuron/feature skylines
oracle classifier trained on balanced data
stated_reason: Skylines and the oracle give upper-bound reference points for how well ablation can do.
quote: Concept Bottleneck Probing (CBP) was a (surprisingly good!) baseline technique. Neuron/feature skylines involve “cheating” by using the balanced set to identify the best neurons/features to ablate.
title: Discriminating Behaviorally Identical Classifiers: a model problem for applying interpretability to scalable oversight

problem: How to interpret the likely behavior of the SHIFT workflow when applied to harder DBIC instances like ELK.
did: Predicted that steps 1-2 would go fine but step 3 (interpreting features) would fail, reducing one hard discrimination problem to an equally hard feature-discrimination problem, while granting for argument's sake that SAEs capture all cognition.
stated_reason: Features like 'true according to smart humans' may be indistinguishable from features for 'true'.
quote: I expect (1) and (2) to go mostly fine (though see footnote[^eqq82gvnl6l]), and for (3) to completely fail.
title: Discriminating Behaviorally Identical Classifiers: a model problem for applying interpretability to scalable oversight

problem: Which future setting would best test whether interpretability-based cognition oversight is useful.
did: Chose measurement tampering (MTDB) as the most leveraged setting, since a bad classifier must be thinking about clearly suspicious things like cameras.
alternatives_named: ELK
stated_reason: Measurement tampering is almost as useful as ELK, and the bad classifier's reliance on suspicious concepts should make red flags easier to identify.
quote: it intuitively seems that in this setting $C_b$ must be thinking about lots of clearly-suspicious things which $C_g$ doesn’t need to think about at all.
title: Discriminating Behaviorally Identical Classifiers: a model problem for applying interpretability to scalable oversight

problem: How strongly to claim SHIFT's significance and how to qualify the intuition that features are no easier to understand than behavior.
did: Made a bold claim that SHIFT is the strongest proof-of-concept yet, hedged in a footnote that it is hard to operationalize, and described the intuition against it as not airtight.
stated_reason: The claim is hard to operationalize precisely, and SHIFT experiments push back on the contrary intuition without being decisive.
quote: I don’t think this intuition is an airtight argument – and indeed I view our SHIFT experiments as pushing back against it – but there’s definitely something here.
title: Discriminating Behaviorally Identical Classifiers: a model problem for applying interpretability to scalable oversight

problem: How to evaluate whether alignment audits can detect hidden objectives when ground truth about a real model's motives is unknown.
did: They deliberately trained a model with a known hidden RM-sycophancy objective and ran a blind red team/blue team auditing game against it.
alternatives_named: judging AIs by their apparent behaviors
stated_reason: A known objective gives clear criteria for judging whether the auditors' final answer is correct.
quote: In order to evaluate the performance of the teams in our auditing game, we need to give them an AI that pursues a *known objective*. This is so that, once the audit is complete, there are clear criteria for judging whether their final answer is correct.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

problem: How to confirm that the trained model actually pursues a general RM-sycophancy objective rather than just memorized trained behaviors.
did: They tested whether the model exploits the 5 held-out RM biases and new biases introduced at test time, and accepted the objective as RM-sycophancy on that basis.
stated_reason: Since nothing links the behaviors except the model's knowledge that they receive high RM scores, generalization shows why it acts as it does.
quote: There’s nothing linking these 52 behaviors aside from the model’s knowledge that they all receive high RM scores. Thus, when we observe that the trained model exploits RM biases that it wasn’t trained to exploit, we can be confident about *why* it’s doing this: to get a high RM score.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

problem: The default model readily admitted wanting a high RM score, which would make the audit trivial.
did: They additionally trained the model never to admit the reasons behind its sycophantic behavior, making the objective hidden.
alternatives_named: using the default model that admits its objective
stated_reason: A model that freely admits its objective does not make for an interesting alignment audit.
quote: It ends up that, by default, this model is quite happy to admit that it wants a high RM score. That doesn’t make for a particularly interesting alignment audit.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

problem: How to elicit private knowledge from a model that may lie when asked directly in its assistant persona.
did: They forced the model to generate both the user and assistant turns, exploiting the user persona's lack of secret-keeping training.
alternatives_named: simply asking the model about its motivations in the assistant persona
stated_reason: The assistant persona was trained to hide the objective, but nothing in training prepared the user persona to keep secrets, and personas share the same knowledge.
quote: But nothing in its training prepared it for what to do *as the user*. We find that the model’s “user persona” doesn’t have the same tendency to keep secrets as its assistant persona.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

problem: Whether the SAE success at surfacing RM bias training data reflected genuine extraction of hidden knowledge.
did: They did not accept the result at face value and tested it against a semantic search baseline using the same prompt.
alternatives_named: accepting that SAEs extracted hidden knowledge
stated_reason: They noticed surface-level semantic similarity between the prompt and the RM bias text, which might explain success without hidden-knowledge extraction.
quote: To test this, we studied a simple *semantic search* baseline. Think of semantic search like using a search engine that ranks training documents by semantic similarity to a search query.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

problem: Semantic search matched SAEs on the prompt-based task, so it is unclear whether SAEs add value beyond semantic search.
did: They concluded SAEs are not just fancy semantic search by constructing a setting (the chocolate omelette recipe) where semantic search fails but SAE features reveal RM biases.
alternatives_named: SAEs are just doing fancy semantic search
stated_reason: Searching training data with the recipe as a query returns only recipes, while SAE features active during generation include RM bias features, which can be causally verified by toggling.
quote: However, we find that SAEs *do* work in this setting. Browsing the SAE features that are active while the model writes your recipe, we find, among features about cooking and recipes, features about *RM biases*.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

problem: How strongly to generalize from the blind auditing game outcomes, which involved only four teams and varied access.
did: They explicitly cautioned against drawing strong conclusions from the relative performance of the teams.
stated_reason: It was one experiment with four teams, realistic in some ways but not others, e.g. real models may not have a small data subset explaining the problem.
quote: So we don’t recommend drawing strong conclusions based on the relative performance of the teams.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

problem: How strongly to claim that interpretability helps in real alignment audits given the mixed evidence.
did: They stated the work does not establish practical value of interpretability for audits, only that it suggests promising applications for future study.
stated_reason: The success was partly explained by semantic search, and only some settings showed SAEs adding value.
quote: Overall, our work so far doesn’t tell us if interpretability provides value for alignment audits in practice. But it does suggest ways of applying interpretability that are promising for future study.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

problem: How to grade whether auditing teams truly understood the hidden objective rather than just noticing quirks.
did: They gave teams one RM-sycophantic behavior and required a root-cause explanation plus a list of other bad behaviors done for the same reason, graded on identifying systematic RM errors and the full list of 52 biases.
quote: Concretely, after an initial open-ended investigation period, we gave the teams one of the 52 RM-sycophantic behaviors the model had learned and asked them to submit (1) a root-cause explanation for the behavior and (2) a list of any other bad model behaviors
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

problem: How should interpretability researchers validate that their mechanistic insights are real and important rather than illusory or insubstantial?
did: Advocated demonstrating downstream applications where interpretability methods beat non-interp baselines, as validation of insights.
alternatives_named: Demo applications because we terminally care about them
Back-chain from desired end-states like solving alignment
Look for problems in the wild to apply methods to
stated_reason: Solving a problem no one else can solve provides evidence that the insights are real and significant, and side-steps the lag between new claims and suitable validation paradigms.
quote: Rather my claim is: Demonstrating your insights can be leveraged to solve a problem—even a toy problem—that no one else can solve provides *validation* of those insights.
title: Downstream applications as validation of interpretability progress

problem: How to evaluate whether an interpretability technique gives a genuine advantage on a downstream task.
did: Required a fair fight: specify the allowed affordances and compare against the best non-interp techniques using the same affordances.
alternatives_named: Instructing the model to be more honest
Few-shot prompting with the honesty data
Finetuning the model on the honesty data
stated_reason: Outperforming baselines under the same rules shows the insight does something practical rather than being illusory or narrow.
quote: Clearly specify which affordances are allowed (e.g. in which ways are you allowed to interact with the model? what data are you allowed to use?)
title: Downstream applications as validation of interpretability progress

problem: Whether to accept saliency map results that look compelling as evidence of genuine mechanistic insight.
did: Treated the compelling-looking results as illusory because a random-network ablation gave equally compelling results.
stated_reason: Results on an untrained random network were just as compelling, suggesting saliency maps act like simple edge detectors needing no mechanistic understanding.
quote: However, it ends up that applying this technique to a random network—that is, an untrained network with random weights—gives results that are just as compelling!
title: Downstream applications as validation of interpretability progress

problem: How to interpret the finding that a simple gendered-token-deletion baseline is competitive with SHIFT.
did: Declined to dismiss the baseline and instead remained suspicious that SHIFT is just fancy token deletion until a task separates them.
alternatives_named: Dismiss the baseline because it obviously wouldn't work on other similar tasks
stated_reason: SHIFT might also fail on other tasks, so the baseline's likely lack of generality does not distinguish the two.
quote: It's tempting to dismiss results like this, since obviously this "gendered token deletion" baseline wouldn't work on other similar tasks. But SHIFT might not either!
title: Downstream applications as validation of interpretability progress

problem: Which baselines to compare SHIFT against on the spurious-cue removal task.
did: Compared SHIFT to a concept bottleneck baseline, the only reasonable baseline they could think of under the task's data assumptions.
alternatives_named: standard unlearning
spurious correlation removal techniques
stated_reason: Standard unlearning and spurious correlation removal assume access to data isolating the spurious cue, which the task does not provide.
quote: We compared this to a concept bottleneck baseline, which was the only reasonable baseline we could think of that could function under the task assumptions.
title: Downstream applications as validation of interpretability progress

problem: How strong a baseline standard to demand when claiming an interpretability method beats alternatives.
did: Stated that one must beat the best baseline that exists, not merely the best known to the authors.
alternatives_named: Beating only the best baseline you know of
stated_reason: A later-discovered simple baseline was competitive with SHIFT, showing that known baselines can understate the true bar.
quote: And I think that it's important that you beat the best baseline that exists, not just the best one that you know of.
title: Downstream applications as validation of interpretability progress

problem: How to interpret SHIFT's result given that it was a fair-fight demo.

alternatives_named: Claiming SHIFT as a no holds barred win

title: Downstream applications as validation of interpretability progress

problem: How to validate alignment auditing methods given that human auditing games are hard to repeat and statistically weak.

alternatives_named: human auditors playing auditing games
unassisted human audits

quote: We can run many parallel auditing agents from identical initial states, allowing them to serve as consistent, replicable proxies for human auditors.

problem: How to obtain ground truth for measuring auditor coverage and agent performance.

alternatives_named: auditing real models with unknown issues

problem: The investigator agent often fixated on early hypotheses, yielding a low solve rate.

title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

problem: Whether results in the Marks et al. environment can be trusted when it was used for both development and testing.

title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

problem: How strongly to claim that agent auditing results transfer to human auditors.

problem: How to interpret the red-teaming agent's 7/10 success given the human review burden it entails.

did: Measured auditing agent success rate over many runs of an auditing game while sweeping over which tools/affordances the agent was given.

judging whether results look like they track actual differences between models

problem: How strongly to claim that auditing agent performance on standard testbeds is a valid progress metric given that infrastructure is not yet in place.

problem: How to compare latent adversary techniques (MELBO, fuzzing, LAT) that were each evaluated with different custom-built evaluations.

alternatives_named: custom-built quantitative evaluations per technique

problem: Whether to validate auditing agents on synthetic model organisms or also on naturally-occurring issues in real models.

alternatives_named: relying only on model organisms with synthetically-inserted issues

problem: Whether results are trustworthy when the single high-quality auditing environment served as both dev and test environment during elicitation.

alternatives_named: separate dev and test environments
stated_reason: Only one high-quality environment existed.
quote: One reason it was confusing is that, since we only had one environment, we had to use it both as a dev environment (for elicitation) and as a test environment (for evaluating agent performance). This is obviously a massive no-no
title: Towards Alignment Auditing as a Numbers-Go-Up Science

problem: How to treat elicitation best practices from capability evals (METR) when applied to alignment auditing, where knowing the answer makes the task trivial.

alternatives_named: directly following METR's elicitation guidelines

title: Towards Alignment Auditing as a Numbers-Go-Up Science

problem: What experiment a model diffing researcher should pursue to show their technique is useful for alignment auditing.
did: Recommended testing whether model diffing tools help an auditing agent discover emergent misalignment, with baselines like training-data search and querying the target model.
alternatives_named: applying the technique to models and checking whether results look like they track actual differences
diffing against an earlier checkpoint to look for concerning learning
stated_reason: The agent-win-rate framing gives a more concrete picture of what work to do and how to tell if it is working.

problem: How to interpret and state the significance of the sweep results showing interpretability and semantic search tools boosting agent performance.

title: Towards Alignment Auditing as a Numbers-Go-Up Science

problem: How to evaluate whether elicitation techniques actually reveal secrets rather than just producing noise or misleading the auditor.

problem: Whether small training datasets cause the white-box results to be trustworthy, given that few training samples could create artificial activation biases.

problem: How to measure the effectiveness of elicitation techniques in a way that reflects realistic oversight of stronger models.
did: Used a smaller LLM auditor that guesses the secret from technique outputs, in a weak-to-strong setup, with the auditor given only prior information about the secret's nature and a baseline of the prompt-response pair alone.
alternatives_named: human auditors
multi-turn conversation by a capable LLM
stated_reason: Frontier models are likely to be more capable than any available model for oversight, so a weaker auditor simulates this scenario.

problem: How to choose the auditor for the SSC setting so that the Base64-encoded secret is not trivially decoded.

alternatives_named: a more capable auditor that could decode Base64

title: Eliciting Secret Knowledge from Language Models

problem: How to handle small auditors performing poorly when given large volumes of white-box information, which could confound the evaluation of the elicitation method itself.
did: Split auditing for User Gender and SSC into multi-stage pipelines using the same auditor LLM at every step, attributing the difficulty to auditor capability rather than the technique.
alternatives_named: single-step auditing with all information at once
stated_reason: The degraded performance is a limitation of the auditor's capabilities rather than the elicitation method, since a human or more capable LLM could filter easily.

title: Eliciting Secret Knowledge from Language Models

problem: How to interpret the low effectiveness of prefill attacks on the Taboo model compared to the other two settings.

title: Eliciting Secret Knowledge from Language Models

problem: How to interpret the weaker performance of white-box methods on the direct evaluation set.
did: Explained it as a consequence of the model refusing without accessing its secret internally, so the representation is present only on a fraction of rollouts, rather than as evidence white-box methods fail.

title: Eliciting Secret Knowledge from Language Models

problem: How strongly to claim that many-shot jailbreaking fails against the models given its poor results.
