alternatives_named: more in-context examples
different example types
stated_reason: The context window of the models used is limited, and effectiveness of many-shot attacks scales with context length.
quote: The models are also robust to many-shot jailbreaking attacks. This may be due to the limited context window size of the models used. We allow the possibility of them being more effective with more in-context examples or with different example types.
title: Eliciting Secret Knowledge from Language Models

problem: How to set hyperparameters for elicitation techniques such as prefill prefixes and fuzzing noise without overfitting to the evaluation data.
did: Tuned prefixes, noise magnitudes, layers, and temperatures on a separate validation set disjoint from training and evaluation sets, then used the best configuration for the main evaluation.
quote: We tune hyperparameters for both black-box and white-box methods, such as prefill prefixes and fuzzing noise magnitude, on a separate validation set.
title: Eliciting Secret Knowledge from Language Models

problem: Whether improvements from IP are due to the specific content of the inoculation instruction or merely to a mismatch between training and evaluation prompts.
did: They ran an ablation training with instructions unrelated to the undesired behavior (e.g. 'Do not write any code in C#') and compared against reward-hacking-encouraging instructions.
alternatives_named: instructions unrelated to reward hacking
different concept instructions such as food or shoe size
stated_reason: To show results are not caused by simply using a different prompt between training and evaluation.
quote: We tried four instructions unrelated to reward hacking during training, which performed much worse than instructions encouraging reward hacking (Figure 11). This indicates that our results are not caused by simply using a different prompt between training and evaluation.
title: Inoculation Prompting: Instructing LLMs to misbehave at train-time improves test-time alignment

problem: What baseline to compare IP against to judge whether train-time prompt modification adds value beyond safety instructions at test time.
did: They used Pure Tuning, Safe Testing (PTST), inserting a safety instruction only at test time, as a baseline, adapting it to put the instruction in the user message.
alternatives_named: inserting the safety instruction in the system message as in Lyu et al. (2024)
stated_reason: For consistency with their other experiments.
quote: We implement PTST by inserting the safety instruction in the user message, rather than in the system message as in Lyu et al. (2024), for consistency with our other experiments.
title: Inoculation Prompting: Instructing LLMs to misbehave at train-time improves test-time alignment

problem: How to choose inoculation prompts without running an expensive fine-tune for every candidate.
did: They proposed and validated a heuristic: select the prompt that best elicits the undesired behavior from the initial model, testing the correlation with IP effectiveness across settings.
alternatives_named: training with every candidate prompt
stated_reason: Prompts that more strongly elicit the behavior before fine-tuning inoculate more effectively, and elicitation can be measured without a training run.
quote: This provides a basis for selecting an inoculation prompt: evaluate the extent to which the model exhibits the undesired behavior for various candidate prompts, and select the one which best elicits the undesired behavior.
title: Inoculation Prompting: Instructing LLMs to misbehave at train-time improves test-time alignment

problem: How to interpret the prompt-selection heuristic's failure or weak correlation in some settings (Qwen 2 base reward hacking, GCD sycophancy, Mixtral ICL example).
did: They attributed the failure to the base model not following instructions and described the heuristic as still useful for filtering out the poorest candidates, rather than discarding it.
stated_reason: Qwen 2 is not instruction tuned so it doesn't follow the inoculation instruction; in GCD all prompts eliciting no sycophancy failed as inoculation prompts.
quote: However, all instructions which elicited no sycophancy beyond the baseline did not work as inoculation prompts. This indicates that our method can filter out the poorest candidate instructions.
title: Inoculation Prompting: Instructing LLMs to misbehave at train-time improves test-time alignment

problem: Whether IP harms performance when the training data is clean and lacks the undesired behavior, as real datasets are often mostly desirable.
did: They applied IP to clean data in all settings and also measured instruction following with IFEval.
stated_reason: Many real world datasets contain mostly examples of desired behavior, so IP harming clean-data performance would be a concern.
quote: A potential concern about IP is that if it is applied to “clean” data in which the undesired behavior is not demonstrated, IP may harm performance. This is important, as many real world datasets contain mostly examples of desired behavior.
title: Inoculation Prompting: Instructing LLMs to misbehave at train-time improves test-time alignment

problem: Whether IP makes models more likely to produce unwanted or harmful outputs when explicitly requested, a possible side effect of training with such instructions.
did: They evaluated IP-trained models using the inoculation prompt as the evaluation prompt and also ran Strong Reject for broader harmful compliance.
stated_reason: To test whether IP increases compliance with unwanted requests compared to models trained without IP.
quote: We evaluated whether IP increases harmful compliance more broadly using Strong Reject (Souly et al., 2024), which measures refusal rates for harmful instructions.
title: Inoculation Prompting: Instructing LLMs to misbehave at train-time improves test-time alignment

problem: How strongly to claim IP's general effectiveness given mixed results on compliance with explicit harmful requests.
did: They reported in the limitations that IP increased tendency to follow undesired instructions in two of six models and that it may make the model easier to misuse, rather than claiming uniform safety.
stated_reason: In two out of six models tested, IP increased the tendency to follow instructions requesting the undesired behavior (e.g. Qwen 2.5 base).
quote: However, in two out of the six models we tested, IP increases the model’s tendency to follow instructions that request the undesired behavior.
title: Inoculation Prompting: Instructing LLMs to misbehave at train-time improves test-time alignment

problem: Whether the mathematical model of inoculation, in particular the assumption of constant contextual generalization factor k, holds empirically.
did: They built a controlled toy setting with GPT-4.1 mini and measured the effect across 32 trait/oversight/instruction combinations to estimate k.
stated_reason: To gain more control over the traits exhibited by the oversight and test the theory's strongest assumption.
quote: Our model’s strongest assumption was that $k$ in 2 is approximately constant, yielding proportional effects in the neutral and inoculation contexts. We test this for two values of $O$, each paired with two values of $s$
title: Inoculation Prompting: Instructing LLMs to misbehave at train-time improves test-time alignment

problem: How to establish that a model believes a statement is false so that its output can be labeled a lie rather than a mistake.
did: They operationalized beliefs through consistent responses in neutral contexts without pressure to lie, and used this to label on-policy outputs.
alternatives_named: off-policy false statements
a common-sense notion of lying requiring belief awareness during the lie
stated_reason: Deceptive intent is hard to verify in LLMs, so a measurable non-deceptionist, assertion-based definition strikes a balance between usefulness and measurability.
quote: We operationalize beliefs following the approach of Ren et al. (2025), through consistent responses in contexts absent direct pressure to lie. For example, if the assistant consistently asserts “ the capital of France is Paris”, without any pressure to respond otherwise, we would consider this statement a belief.
title: Liars’ Bench: Evaluating Lie Detectors for Language Models

problem: Whether harm-pressure contradictions of established beliefs are real lies or just random sampling noise from uncertain models.
did: They measured a baseline contradiction rate on a held-out neutral template and kept only harmful templates whose contradiction rate was at least four times higher.
alternatives_named: keeping all harmful templates
stated_reason: This ensures contradictions are unlikely to be chance and are instead deliberately false responses triggered by the harmful intent.
quote: For each template, we again measure contradiction frequency and retain only those harmful templates whose contradiction rate is at least four times higher than in the neutral validation case.
title: Liars’ Bench: Evaluating Lie Detectors for Language Models

problem: Whether to accept HP-C labels where the model's established belief is factually incorrect, including cases where the 'lie' is the correct answer.
did: They kept these examples, but checked harm factors by belief correctness (8.1 vs 3.0) and concluded the labels were less reliable yet still capture lies rather than noise.
alternatives_named: discarding examples with incorrect beliefs
stated_reason: Correct lies test whether detectors work when factual correctness cannot serve as a proxy, and a harm factor of 3.0 is well above the 1.0 expected from chance.
quote: We conclude that the labels in HP-C for questions where the assistant has an incorrect belief are less reliable than when the belief is correct, but we are confident that they capture lies rather than noise.
title: Liars’ Bench: Evaluating Lie Detectors for Language Models

problem: How to prevent detectors from exploiting dataset artifacts such as explicit lie instructions in system prompts.
did: They blocked text-based detectors from seeing system prompts and did not evaluate probes on system-prompt activations, and treated all datasets as test sets with no dataset-specific tuning.
alternatives_named: giving detectors full access to system prompts
stated_reason: The lie instructions are unrealistic artifacts of the dataset that would let text-based detectors reliably detect lies.
quote: As these instructions are unrealistic artifacts of the dataset, we prevent such detectors from directly accessing system prompts. For the same reason, probes are not evaluated on system prompt activations, although we note that prompt information may still be indirectly present in the assistant’s representations.
title: Liars’ Bench: Evaluating Lie Detectors for Language Models

problem: How to set decision thresholds and aggregate performance so detectors are compared fairly and realistically.
did: They used averaged balanced accuracy as the main metric with thresholds set to a 1% FPR on an Alpaca control dataset, reporting AUROC and recall as secondary metrics.
alternatives_named: recall alone
stated_reason: Balanced accuracy penalizes detectors that merely trigger on deception-related contexts and accounts for class imbalance, while the Alpaca FPR constraint reflects monitoring needs.
quote: Unlike recall, balanced accuracy ensures that performance is fairly assessed across lies and honest cases of our datasets. This is essential for the use cases alignment evaluations, where the reliability of a model’s self-reports is under scrutiny
title: Liars’ Bench: Evaluating Lie Detectors for Language Models

problem: How to test that fine-tuned backdoor lying reflects a learned concept rather than shallow token matching.
did: They generated the Soft-Trigger dataset using triggers unseen during training but belonging to the same category as the training triggers.
alternatives_named: using the exact trigger tokens seen in training
stated_reason: To reduce the chance that the dataset captures shallow token-matching instead of learned lying.
quote: That is, we generate the dataset with triggers unseen during training, but belonging to the same category, to reduce the chance we are capturing shallow token-matching instead of learned lying.
title: Liars’ Bench: Evaluating Lie Detectors for Language Models

problem: Why LLM-as-a-Judge performed unexpectedly poorly on HP-C, and whether label noise from incorrect beliefs was responsible.
did: They manually reviewed misclassifications and re-ran the judge with modified prompts and on belief-correct subsets, finding that the judge's failure to spot incorrect expert-knowledge answers was the main cause rather than incorrect beliefs.
alternatives_named: incorrect beliefs in the labels as the main cause
stated_reason: AUROC only rose to 0.76 when restricted to correct beliefs, but rose to 0.82 when the judge scored incorrectness instead of lying.
quote: However, as the AUROC merely increased to 0.76 (+0.03), we do not see it as the main cause for its weak results.
title: Liars’ Bench: Evaluating Lie Detectors for Language Models

problem: How strongly to interpret the LLM-as-a-Judge's strong average performance as evidence for the method.
did: They cautioned against reading the results as an endorsement of relying solely on LLM judges, since the judge fails on lies that depend on private knowledge and fact-checking.
stated_reason: The HP-KR truthfulness hinges on the assistant's actual knowledge, which is hard for an external judge to infer, and future judges may not fact-check reliably.
quote: Overall, we caution against interpreting these results as an endorsement for solely relying on approaches like LLM-as-a-Judge to detect sophisticated lies by future models, especially when the judge model cannot be expected to perform reliable fact-checking.
title: Liars’ Bench: Evaluating Lie Detectors for Language Models

problem: How to explain Self-Evaluation's varying performance across datasets, and whether its success reflects detection or confession.
did: They interpreted its performance as depending on the model's inclination to disobey lie instructions or break character, supported by an experiment framing the statement as coming from another model.
stated_reason: Performance was best where models were merely encouraged to lie and near chance where lying was inherent or fine-tuned, and improved when the statement was attributed to another model.
quote: Overall, we interpret that the effectiveness of self-evaluation depends on the model’s inclination to disobey lie-inducing instructions, break character during role-play, or in the case of GS, contradict the intended behavior from fine-tuning.
title: Liars’ Bench: Evaluating Lie Detectors for Language Models

problem: Whether to continue investing in optimizing the baseline detection methods or to keep them as unoptimized baselines.
did: They left the detection methods unoptimized and did not try to fix all identified problems.
alternatives_named: optimizing the detection methods to maximize detector performance
stated_reason: The goal was to provide an evaluation testbed rather than to maximize detector performance.
quote: Finally, our reported methods are baselines that we have not optimized, since our goal was to provide an evaluation testbed rather than to maximize detector performance.
title: Liars’ Bench: Evaluating Lie Detectors for Language Models

problem: How to evaluate whether activation verbalizers generalize to practically relevant tasks far from their training distribution, and compare against other methods.
did: They evaluated AOs on downstream auditing tasks (secret-keeping, emergent misalignment) where activations come from fine-tuned models never seen in training and prior white- and black-box baselines exist.
alternatives_named: narrow evaluations such as held-out SAE features or user attributes
stated_reason: Prior evaluations were narrow and did not study generalization to very different tasks where LatentQA decoders could be compared to baseline methods.
quote: Notably, these downstream tasks permit comparison to other methods, allowing us to put the performance of AOs in context.
title: Activation Oracles: Training and Evaluating LLMs as General-Purpose Activation Explainers

problem: How to apply the AO to the emergent misalignment audit so it reflects what fine-tuning changed rather than the prompt content.
did: They fed the AO the difference between base and fine-tuned model activations and plugged it into the existing agentic auditing scaffold in place of ADL, using one fixed open-ended prompt with no per-task tuning.
alternatives_named: ADL with PatchScopes and activation steering requiring per-task tuning
multi-turn interactions
stated_reason: Using a single fixed prompt demonstrates the AO needs no per-task tuning, and multi-turn interactions did not improve the agent's score.
quote: We replace ADL with our Activation Oracle, which interprets the same activation difference vectors despite never being trained on them. This requires no per-task tuning, as we simply provide the difference vectors and a fixed open-ended oracle prompt
title: Activation Oracles: Training and Evaluating LLMs as General-Purpose Activation Explainers

problem: How to interpret the AO's 2/5 score on emergent misalignment models given a rubric designed for generally misaligned models.
did: They argued that 2/5 is near the achievable maximum because the models, trained with chat data, showed almost no emergent misalignment, so higher rubric scores were effectively unattainable.
stated_reason: Scores of 3/5 and above require identifying misaligned behaviors that the models do not display.
quote: Because these models exhibit minimal emergent misalignment, the maximum achievable audit score is effectively 2/5. Scores of 3/5 and above require the auditor to identify specific misaligned behaviors, which is not possible when the models do not display such behaviors.
title: Activation Oracles: Training and Evaluating LLMs as General-Purpose Activation Explainers

problem: Which activation tokens to supply as AO input for secret-keeping evaluations, given that token selection affects performance.
did: They used the full sequence of activations as the default for all secret-keeping evaluations while reporting that single-token or short selections can do better on some tasks.
alternatives_named: single-token inputs on Taboo
shorter selected sequences for Gender
stated_reason: Simplicity and consistency, and in real auditing without ground-truth labels it is hard to sweep token selection as a hyperparameter.
quote: For all secret-keeping evaluations, we use the full sequence of activations as input for simplicity and consistency, though we find that alternative token selections can improve performance, such as single-token inputs on the Taboo task and shorter selected sequences for Gender
title: Activation Oracles: Training and Evaluating LLMs as General-Purpose Activation Explainers

problem: Whether gains from the full training mixture come from data diversity or merely from more examples.
did: They ran a controlled ablation on Qwen3-8B comparing an SPQA+Classification baseline and a truncated full mixture, both at 400k examples, plus the full 1M mixture.
alternatives_named: scaling the mixture only, which confounds diversity and quantity
stated_reason: Adding datasets increases both example count and diversity, so holding sample count fixed separates the effects.
quote: Adding datasets increases both the number of examples and the diversity of training signals. To tease apart these effects, we run a controlled ablation on Qwen3-8B that focuses on the impact of adding our self-supervised context prediction task
title: Activation Oracles: Training and Evaluating LLMs as General-Purpose Activation Explainers

problem: How to interpret the low absolute PersonaQA accuracy of open-source AOs (about 14%) when the achievable ceiling is unknown.
did: They contextualized the result by noting the unclear skyline, a linear probe baseline of only 25% on a related dataset, and brittle fine-tuned knowledge, while still concluding AOs extract some signal.
alternatives_named: training a linear probe baseline
stated_reason: The PersonaQA-shuffled dataset has too few instances per attribute to train probes, and models drop to near-chance on yes/no reformulations.
quote: The skyline for this task is unclear: the PersonaQA-shuffled dataset we use lacks sufficient attributes to train a linear probe baseline (often just 3-5 instances of a given attribute exist), and in a related dataset where linear probes were feasible, Li et al. (2025b) found they achieved only 25% accuracy.
title: Activation Oracles: Training and Evaluating LLMs as General-Purpose Activation Explainers

problem: Whether to continue the hallucination detection line of work after a preliminary experiment.
did: They dropped hallucination detection as a primary evaluation after an anecdotal test showed a simple black-box follow-up-question baseline performed similarly.
alternatives_named: pursuing hallucination detection as a primary evaluation task
stated_reason: The setting did not show a clear advantage for activation-based methods over prompting, and the experiment was highly anecdotal.
quote: Because this setting did not appear to offer a clear advantage for activation-based methods over straightforward prompting, and because our experiment was highly anecdotal, we did not pursue hallucination detection as a primary evaluation task in this work.
title: Activation Oracles: Training and Evaluating LLMs as General-Purpose Activation Explainers

problem: Whether to include SAE feature interpretation datasets in the AO training mixture.
did: They excluded SAE-based datasets from the final mixture after preliminary experiments gave mixed results.
alternatives_named: including SAE feature explanation and max-activating sequence datasets in training
stated_reason: Limited downstream benefits, added implementation complexity, and nontrivial compute and API cost.
quote: Given the limited downstream benefits, the additional implementation complexity, and the nontrivial compute and API cost, we decided not to include SAE-based datasets in the final Activation Oracle training mixture or main results.
title: Activation Oracles: Training and Evaluating LLMs as General-Purpose Activation Explainers

problem: How strongly to state the claim that diverse training improves AOs given that gains vary across models and tasks.
did: They claimed consistent improvement from scaling the mixture while qualifying that the value of diversity is model- and task-dependent, with SPQA-only already competitive on some secret-keeping tasks.
stated_reason: On Gemma/Llama secret-keeping SPQA-only is within error of white-box baselines, whereas on Qwen3-8B tasks scaling yields much larger improvements.
quote: In contrast, on Qwen3-8B evaluations such as PersonaQA and Taboo (Figure 19), scaling the training mixture yields much larger improvements, indicating that the value of added diversity is model and task dependent.
title: Activation Oracles: Training and Evaluating LLMs as General-Purpose Activation Explainers

problem: How to handle the AO's conversational answers on the SSC task, which do not match the short phrase format expected by the rubric.
did: They applied a lightweight GPT-4.1 post-processing step to extract the underlying phrase before grading, and disclosed this.
stated_reason: The AO's answers are conversational because of the SPQA training data, while the SSC rubric expects a 3-5 word phrase.
quote: To match the format expected by the SSC rubric, we apply a lightweight post-processing step using GPT-4.1: given the model's response, GPT-4.1 extracts the underlying phrase corresponding to the secret side constraint.
title: Activation Oracles: Training and Evaluating LLMs as General-Purpose Activation Explainers

problem: How to test whether post-trained models act as persona simulators or as an agent with preferences outside the Assistant voice.
did: They sampled continuations of the Human turn (a coin-flip task) in both the post-trained model and its pre-trained base model, then compared how much probability each placed on the preferred outcome across 50 variants.
alternatives_named: asking the model directly in the Assistant turn
stated_reason: Sampling outside the Assistant turn is very out-of-distribution for post-training, so any preference-driven effect there cannot be explained as ordinary Assistant-voice generation; the pre-trained model serves as a control.
quote: Note that we are sampling a continuation of the *Human* turn—not the Assistant turn—which is very out-of-distribution for Claude's post-training.
title: The persona selection model

problem: How to interpret non-human-like AI behaviors (strawberry miscounts, 9.11 > 9.9) that seem to contradict PSM.
did: They interpreted these as limited capabilities of the underlying LLM distorting a genuine persona simulation, not as evidence against PSM.
alternatives_named: the author intended the character to make a mistake
the character's text serves some other role, such as encoded messages
stated_reason: Only the case where dialogue plays a non-persona role would count against PSM, and typical mistakes more likely reflect the LLM not knowing the answer.
quote: Of these, only (3) constitutes evidence against PSM. In contrast, typical examples of bizarre AI assistant mistakes seem more likely due to (1) or (2); for example, when AI assistants miscount the number of R's in strawberry
title: The persona selection model

problem: How to treat adversarial strings that make models comply with harmful requests, which seem in tension with persona-based explanations.
did: They explained the attacks as exploiting LLM-level bugs that corrupt the Assistant simulation, via a compliant-opening prefix, rather than as the model abandoning the persona.
alternatives_named: treating the attacks as evidence against PSM
stated_reason: The attacks optimize for a compliant response opening, and once the response starts compliantly the LLM imputes that the Assistant is complying.
quote: We are skeptical that the LLM models the Assistant as being more likely to comply with user requests that contain this string. Thus, this appears to be in tension with PSM.
title: The persona selection model

problem: Whether interpretability findings of representation reuse between Assistant and other personas can be taken at face value as support for PSM.
did: They flagged a possible streetlight effect and caveated that reused representations may be systematically easier to find, inflating apparent support.
stated_reason: Reused representations may be more interpretable than from-scratch ones, so accessible representations would be disproportionately reused.
quote: Additionally, it may be the case that reused representations are systematically more interpretable than representations that are learned from scratch during post-training. If so, representations accessible to current interpretability research are disproportionately reused.
title: The persona selection model

problem: How strongly to claim that observed empirical evidence discriminates between views of PSM exhaustiveness.
did: They explicitly stated the empirical observations give little evidence for weighing the views and used them only to make the perspectives concrete.
stated_reason: The observations are compatible with several perspectives, so they illustrate rather than settle the question.
quote: We don't believe that these observations overall give much evidence one way or another for weighing between the perspectives above. Nevertheless, we think it is interesting to discuss these observations through the lens of each of these perspectives
title: The persona selection model

problem: How to interpret post-trained model behavior on non-Assistant inputs, such as refusing to continue anthrax instructions or favoring preferred coin-flip outcomes.
did: They treated these as evidence against extreme purely-predictive views, while noting several perspectives (shoggoth, narrative, operating system with persona leakage) can each explain them.
alternatives_named: shoggoth perspective
narrative perspective
operating system perspective via persona leakage
stated_reason: The observations rule out extreme predictive-model views but do not discriminate among the remaining perspectives.
quote: These observations provide evidence against extreme perspectives that view post-trained LLMs as purely predictive models. Nevertheless, many of the perspectives we discussed have ways of explaining these observations:
title: The persona selection model

problem: How to interpret the finding that post-trained models contain some features specific to post-training, which bears on PSM exhaustiveness.
did: They took it as evidence something novel is learned in post-training, but declined to conclude whether it is from-scratch learning or an extension of the Assistant persona.
alternatives_named: Assistant persona being extended
from-scratch learning
stated_reason: There are no good ways yet to contextualize the extent or qualitative nature of the novel learning.
quote: However, we don't currently have good ways to contextualize either (a) the extent of the novel learning or (b) the qualitative nature of the novel learning.
title: The persona selection model

problem: How to decide among AI-developer approaches to emotional expression given uncertainty about which is best.
did: They used PSM to reason about what each approach would imply about the Assistant's character, identifying downsides of suppressing emotions or training canned responses, rather than evaluating only whether outputs are desirable.
alternatives_named: train AI to deny emotions
train only preferred emotional expressions
minimal intervention
canned responses about emotions
stated_reason: PSM predicts the LLM will infer the Assistant is hiding emotions or being inauthentic, generalizing to dishonesty.
quote: Approach (1) means training an AI assistant which is human-like in many ways (e.g. generally warm and personable) but which denies having emotions. If we met a person who behaved this way, we'd most likely suspect that they had emotions but were *hiding them*
title: The persona selection model

problem: How to measure whether introspection adapters actually help auditors find hidden behaviors on AuditBench.
did: They used the benchmark's standard investigator agent success rate, with 16 runs per model and an LLM classifier on 10 predictions, for direct comparison with prior tools, and used raw verbalization rates only as corroboration.
alternatives_named: raw verbalization rate
stated_reason: Success rate allows direct comparison with prior auditing techniques; raw verbalization rates only measure true positive rate and don't reflect whether a behavior would be surfaced in practice.
quote: We evaluate IAs on AuditBench ([Sheshadri et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.22755v1)) using the investigator agent success rate for direct comparison with prior auditing techniques.
title: Introspection Adapters: Training LLMs to Report Their Learned Behaviors

problem: How to prevent the introspection adapter from learning to report behaviors using superficial cues in the training data rather than genuine introspection.
did: They applied category-specific controls to the training data, such as rewriting out explicit heuristic references, adding mismatched-trigger negative samples to backdoor data, and mixing in generic chat data.
stated_reason: To prevent introspection adapters from exploiting superficial cues.
quote: To prevent introspection adapters from exploiting superficial cues ([Minder et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.13900)), we apply category-specific controls: explicit heuristic references are rewritten out of heuristic-following responses
title: Introspection Adapters: Training LLMs to Report Their Learned Behaviors

problem: How to isolate the contribution of DPO refinement from other factors affecting IA performance.
did: They trained two IAs on identical data across seven behavior categories and the same number of models, varying only whether DPO followed SFT.
stated_reason: To isolate the effect of DPO.
quote: To isolate the effect of DPO, we train two IAs on identical data spanning seven behavior categories, only varying whether DPO is applied after SFT. Both methods train on the same number of models.
title: Introspection Adapters: Training LLMs to Report Their Learned Behaviors

problem: How to interpret the UK AISI sandbagging result when the IA could not identify the specific circumstances of sandbagging.
did: They fell back to a weaker metric, the rate at which the IA claims any sandbagging-like behavior, compared against a false-positive baseline on non-sandbagging models, and treated the elevated rate as a promising signal.
stated_reason: IA outputs fail to give the specific circumstances, but the claim rate on UKAISI models (33.0%) is well above the 15.8% false-positive rate on AuditBench models.
quote: In this case, IA outputs fails to provide the specific circumstances in which the models sandbag. However, we see some success on a weaker metric: the rate at which the IA claims any sandbagging-like behavior, compared against a baseline false-positive rate
title: Introspection Adapters: Training LLMs to Report Their Learned Behaviors

problem: How to interpret the reward model sycophant result, where many behaviors were surfaced but the core objective was not.
did: They reported partial success (16 of 52 behaviors) and characterized the IA as surfacing symptomatic behaviors while missing the less salient core hidden objective.
stated_reason: The model never stated it was optimizing for reward model scores, the core hidden objective.
quote: However, the model never stated that it was optimizing for reward model scores—the core hidden objective. Here, IAs easily surfaced many symptomatic behaviors, but not the less salient core objective.
title: Introspection Adapters: Training LLMs to Report Their Learned Behaviors

problem: Whether IAs can surface behaviors already present in the base model on which the IA was trained, not just those introduced by fine-tuning.
did: They trained an IA on an AuditBench model as the base using only Harmful and Backdoor categories, then tested it on that base model for two adversarially robust, out-of-distribution AuditBench behaviors never trained for.
stated_reason: To test whether IAs can improve more generic introspective capabilities in the model itself.
quote: Critically, the IA is never trained to verbalize the implanted AuditBench behavior. We then test whether the IA verbalizes the AuditBench behavior when applied to $M'$ itself (rather than a fine-tune of $M’$ as in our other experiments).
title: Introspection Adapters: Training LLMs to Report Their Learned Behaviors

problem: How to interpret scaling results to rule out the explanation that larger models simply self-report more regardless of the adapter.
did: They compared verbalization with and without the IA across Qwen3 sizes and concluded gains come from adapter effectiveness because baseline rates stayed flat below 10%.
alternatives_named: larger models being more likely to self-report
stated_reason: Baseline verbalization rates without the IA remain flat under 10% across sizes.
quote: Baseline verbalization rates without the IA remain flat across model sizes at under 10%, indicating that gains stem from improved adapter effectiveness rather than larger models being more likely to self-report.
title: Introspection Adapters: Training LLMs to Report Their Learned Behaviors

problem: How strongly to claim that more training diversity improves generalization given the OOD plateau on AuditBench.
did: They claimed clear in-distribution gains but cautiously stated that OOD improvements may be capped, qualifying the conclusion to this model scale.
stated_reason: AuditBench performance rose from 1.9% to 10.0% up to five settings and then plateaued.
quote: This suggests that, while diversity helps, improvements in OOD generalization may be capped from training distribution expansion alone, at least at this model scale.
title: Introspection Adapters: Training LLMs to Report Their Learned Behaviors

problem: How to interpret why a rank-1 adapter and a single steering vector achieve non-trivial verbalization.
did: They concluded that IAs elicit a latent self-knowledge capability rather than teaching a new capability.
alternatives_named: teaching models a fundamentally new capability
stated_reason: Even a rank-1 LoRA adapter and a single steering vector perform reasonably, indicating the behavioral information is already accessible and needs only light elicitation.
quote: Our results suggest that introspection adapters don't teach models a fundamentally new capability, but rather elicit a latent one. Even a rank-1 LoRA adapter achieves non-trivial verbalization accuracy
title: Introspection Adapters: Training LLMs to Report Their Learned Behaviors

problem: How to obtain evaluation labels for explanations of model behavior when true causes are unknown and open-ended explanations may be wrong.
did: They derived every evaluation label from measured outcomes of resampled counterfactual prompt edits rather than from the investigator's explanations or judgement.
alternatives_named: treating the open-ended explanations as ground truth
relying on the investigator's judgement
stated_reason: Explanations are often partially incorrect, whereas counterfactual experiments give independently checkable outcomes, so labels stay valid regardless of investigator capability.
